The solicitor should accept, as the solicitor is likely to be able to juggle the two files. After all, the partner has assured the solicitor that the case is a straightforward one.
The solicitor should accept the instructions, as this would most likely enhance the solicitor’s chances at the appraisal.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.2_ Overview of Principles and Codes Part 2

questions.question_text: You are employed in a small law firm which specialises in family matters. You recently acted for a local celebrity in relation to a high-profile divorce. There was a lot of press interest and coverage of the divorce, which resulted in the celebrity securing a particularly good divorce settlement. As a result, you were interviewed by the local newspaper and radio stations. Since then, there have been a remarkably high number of enquiries from potential new clients wanting you (or your firm) to represent them in their own divorce proceedings. You and the partners in your firm have agreed you need to recruit two solicitors to the firm, three paralegals and an administrative assistant to help with the increased workload. In relation to existing and new staff, which one of the following categories is outside the data the SRA requires monitored?
options: Disability status of staff.
Whether staff attended private or state schools.
Religion of staff.
The classification of degree awarded.
The classification of degree awarded. Gender of staff.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.2_ Overview of Principles and Codes Part 2

questions.question_text: You are an assistant solicitor in a medium-sized law firm. You are working for a partner who is also the firm’s appointed Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP). They ask you to consider how Principle 4 (the duty to act with honesty) may affect the practice. Which of the following scenarios falls outside the scope of Principle 4?
options: A solicitor is chatting to a potential new client at a networking event. The client tells the solicitor that they have a box at Manchester City and invite the solicitor to watch a game with them. The solicitor indicates they are a Manchester City fan and would enjoy that. In fact, the solicitor supports Chelsea.

A solicitor applied for a job at a new firm. They know that the new firm is competitive and prestigious, so the solicitor adds some extra experience to their CV. They also changed their degree classification from a 2:1 to a 1st.
A solicitor has a short-term cash flow problem. They are unable to pay their staff wages. They borrow money from a client account in the sum of £20,000 and repay the money 3 days later.

A solicitor realises they have missed a court order for directions in a commercial contract litigated case. The solicitor was supposed to exchange witness statements on 2 March 20xx. The solicitor sends the witness statements to the other side on the 5 March 20xx but backdates the letter to date it as of 2 March 20xx.

A solicitor has a personal injury case for an elderly client. The client slipped in a local store on wet flooring. The insurers are denying the claim and the solicitor believes they have grounds for the denial. The solicitor has known the client for years and doesn’t want to upset them. The solicitor tells the client that the claim is going well in the hopes that they may be able to persuade the insurers to settle the claim.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.2_ Overview of Principles and Codes Part 2

questions.question_text: You are acting for a client in a commercial litigation dispute. The matter is heavily contested by both parties and is now in the process of litigation. During the process for disclosure, your client forwards you an internal quality control report which is damaging to your client’s case and helpful to their opponent’s case. You inform the client that under the rules for disclosure the document must be disclosed. Your client refuses saying it is their internal report and the other side do not even know it exists and so cannot request it. Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: Where two Principles appear to conflict with each other, you must follow the Principle which acts in your clients best interests and therefore you cannot disclose the document and you must continue to act.

Where two Principles appear to conflict with each other, you must follow the Principle which serves the wider interest and therefore considering Principle 1 and 7 you must decline to act if the client refuses to disclose the document.
The client is asking you to breach Principles 1, 4 and 5. You must therefore inform the client that you are going to disclose the document so that you do not breach your code of conduct.

Where two Principles appear to conflict with each other, you must follow the Principle which serves the wider interest and therefore considering Principle 1 and 7 you must disclose the document so that you are not in breach of the Codes of Conduct.
Under Principle 7, your duty to act in the client’s best interests mean you cannot disclose the document and you may continue to act.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.2_ Overview of Principles and Codes Part 2

cond3.3.stem: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client in a litigation matter. At the hearing, the client loses the case and is ordered to pay £5,000 towards the opponent’s costs. Outside court the solicitor says to their opponent, “Don’t worry. I’ll make sure that the £5,000 will be paid within the next 14 days.” Fourteen days have now elapsed, and the client has still not provided the solicitor with any funds to pay the costs. Who can force the solicitor to comply with the promise?
options: Legal Ombudsman.
The court.
No one.
Solicitors Disciplinary Tribunal.
Solicitors Regulatory Authority.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor in a sole practice has been found with a small amount of Class A drugs at a house party. The solicitor has accepted a caution for the offence. Which of the following best describes the professional conduct implications in the circumstances?
options: The solicitor has not breached any conduct regulations given that the offence is minor and only attracted a caution.
The solicitor has breached the conduct regulations but only to a minor extent and there is no obligation to self-report.
The solicitor has breached the conduct regulations because a criminal offence has been committed.
The solicitor is in breach of the conduct regulations as the solicitor has failed to uphold public trust and confidence in the profession.
The solicitor has not breached any conduct regulations as the incident happened at a house party, as opposed to in a professional context.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The deadline for serving a witness statement on the other party was yesterday. The solicitor has not been able to get a signed copy from the client. The solicitor receives a telephone call from the opposing solicitor, who is furious that the statement was not served on time and who threatens to issue an urgent application to the court. To calm the opposing solicitor down, the solicitor tells them not to worry and that they will serve the statement by 10am tomorrow. Which of the following best explains the solicitor’s professional conduct position?
options: The solicitor has acted dishonestly in making a promise which could not be met.
The solicitor has given an undertaking which is binding upon the solicitor personally.

There are no professional conduct issues because the promise was just to prevent the other solicitor from making an application that would escalate the costs in the case, which would have been borne by the client.
There are no professional conduct issues because the discussion was not confirmed in writing.
There are no professional conduct issues because the promise was too ambiguous to be construed as an undertaking.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a defendant in a personal injury matter. The case is settled on the basis that the defendant will pay damages of £10,000. The solicitor undertakes that the £10,000 will be paid within seven days. The firm’s policy is that when an undertaking is given, a written note must be placed on the client’s file. The solicitor puts a written note on the file and then goes away on two weeks’ holiday. No one from the firm looks at the file in the solicitor’s absence and consequently the £10,000 is not paid on the due date. Which of the following best describes who has breached the Code of Conduct?
options: The firm’s managers bear ultimate responsibility and so they alone have breached the Code of Conduct.
The solicitor, the firm and the COLP are all in breach of the Code of Conduct.
The solicitor is not in breach of the Code of Conduct because they have complied with the firm’s policy.
The solicitor, as the person who gave the undertaking, alone has breached the Code of Conduct.
The firm’s compliance officer for legal practice (COLP) bears ultimate responsibility and so they alone have breached the Code of Conduct.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for the claimant in a litigation matter. The defendant is unrepresented. On the journey for the final hearing, the solicitor is reading a legal journal and discovers that the solicitor has overlooked a case which completely ruins the client’s case. What should the solicitor do on arrival at court?
options: The solicitor should tell the client that the case cannot proceed because of a procedural irregularity.
The solicitor should immediately cease to act on behalf of the client concerned.
The solicitor should discuss with the client the need for them to draw the court’s attention to the case.
The solicitor should ask the client’s consent to draw the case to the court’s attention.
The solicitor should provide the defendant with the name of the case and its citation.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a client in an employment tribunal case. The client had been sacked by their employer for allegedly stealing a laptop. The client is making a claim for unfair dismissal. During cross-examination, the client denies that they ever had the laptop in their possession. Later that day, the client confides in the solicitor that they took the laptop and sold it to a friend to fund a holiday. What should the solicitor do?
options: The solicitor must cease to act because the solicitor cannot knowingly mislead the tribunal.

The solicitor must continue to act but tell the tribunal what the client had said because keeping quiet would be a breach of the solicitor’s duty to act in a way which upholds the proper administration of justice.
The solicitor must disclose the new information to the tribunal and then cease to act because this accords with the solicitor’s duty to uphold the proper administration of justice.
The solicitor should continue to act and remain quiet about the disclosure because the solicitor will not mislead the tribunal by remaining silent.
The solicitor must continue to represent the client because the solicitor’s duty to act in the best interests of the client overrides the solicitor’s duty not to mislead the tribunal.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An in-house solicitor is advising the employer, X Plc, in relation to a dispute. X Plc is anxious that the disclosure process may reveal information damaging to its position. The solicitor is asked by the employer to see what they can do. What should the solicitor do?
options: Do as the client instructs because the solicitor’s duty to act in the best interests of the client overrides the solicitor’s duty to the court.
Tell the client that their duties to the court outweigh their obligations to the client. If the employer-client remains unwilling to disclose all documents, the solicitor must cease to act.

Continue to act but tell the court that certain documents have been withheld because keeping quiet would be a breach of the solicitor’s duty to act in a way which upholds the proper administration of justice.
Continue to act but advise X Plc of its legal obligations to disclose all relevant documents, including those which adversely affect its case. It is then up to X Plc to comply or not.
Continue to act but refuse to confirm or deny knowledge of the existence of information that is damaging to the client’s position because the solicitor would not mislead the court by keeping quiet.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor represents a builder who sustained an accident at work. Last year, the solicitor represented the builder in relation to injuries sustained in a road traffic accident. The medical report attributes injuries to the recent accident at work that the solicitor knows were sustained in the prior road traffic accident. The expert was not informed of the prior accident by either the solicitor or the client. Which of the following best represents the solicitors’ professional conduct obligations?
options: The solicitor does not need to mention anything to the client, the expert witness, the court, or the other side as the solicitor’s duty is to represent the client.
The solicitor must tell the court and the other side that the solicitor considers the expert’s report to be flawed.
The solicitor does not need to mention anything to the client, the expert witness, the court, or the other side as the solicitor is not a medical professional.

The solicitor is obligated to inform the client that the expert report cannot be used unless the expert that prepared the report is properly informed of the underlying facts and the report is amended or another report is obtained.
The solicitor cannot represent the client, as there is a conflict of interest.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor was instructed by a client who is a defendant in a mortgage possession claim, to represent the client at a hearing. The client instructed the solicitor to oppose the possession claim on the basis that their circumstances have now changed, and they are in a position financially to resume payments of the mortgage instalments and pay an additional amount each month to address the accrued arrears. At the hearing, the judge adjourned the hearing for the defendant to file and serve written evidence of the change in circumstances within a specified timeframe. The solicitor forgot to comply with the court order on time and, at the adjourned hearing, the case was further adjourned for the defendant to comply with the order. Can the court make an adverse costs order against the solicitor in favour of the claimant?
options: Yes, but the court can only make such a costs order if the solicitor has been qualified for at least 3 years prior.
Yes, the court has jurisdiction to discipline the solicitor in respect of costs within any matter before the court.
No, the court has jurisdiction to discipline the solicitor but the court can only make a costs order in favour of the solicitor’s client – the defendant. See 3.3.3 and 3.1.8.1.
No, the only way to discipline the solicitor is to refer the solicitor to the Legal Ombudsman.
No, only the SRA has jurisdiction to discipline the solicitor in this matter.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A new client comes in to see a solicitor. The client is the owner of a company which is in dispute with another company over a delivery of defective goods. This is an area of law with which the solicitor is familiar and competent to give advice. The client needs the advice by 2pm today. The solicitor is going on annual leave at 1pm today. The firm is a two- partner firm, and the other partner specialises solely in immigration law. The firm is reluctant to lose the client. Which of the following best describes what the solicitor should do?
options: Accept the instructions and quickly rush through the advice and submit it to the client as quickly as possible.
Decline the instructions, as they are incapable of adequately taking on the work required.

Explain to the client why they cannot act for the client, but make it clear that they will consider cancelling their holiday to offer the advice if the client is willing to pay them three times their usual hourly rate.
Accept the instructions and pass the file on to the other partner to draft the advice for the client, to avoid any rushed advice.
Accept the instructions but go for their annual leave and draft the advice on their return from leave.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.3: Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

cond3.4.stem: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is the senior partner of a law firm that has had its case load taken over by the County Court for management. It has emerged that the firm took on several cases in personal injury, even though their specialism is conveyancing. The firm employs two junior solicitors to handle all personal injury claims. The employees have failed to manage the cases appropriately, missing a number of court deadlines and failing to obtain medical evidence in some cases. They have also made misleading statements to the court and in some cases falsified documents to cover up the fact that documents have not been filed on time. There is a chaotic system of case management and minimal supervision at the firm. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications for the senior partner in the circumstances?
options: The solicitors have acted dishonestly and without integrity by falsifying the documents and misleading the court.
The solicitors have breached conduct regulations by failing to act in the best interests of their clients.
Although not personally involved in handling the cases, the senior partner has breached professional conduct regulations by failing to supervise the solicitors and the conduct of the cases.
There are no professional conduct implications for the senior partner because they did not handle the cases personally.
The solicitors have breached conduct regulations by taking on cases outside of their competence.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person is one of two partners of an SRA-regulated firm and its compliance officer for finance and administration (COFA). The COFA has employed a solicitor at the firm, despite the fact that the solicitor was struck off the roll by the Solicitors' Disciplinary Tribunal for financial misconduct. The COFA is aware that the solicitor also used funds held in trust for a client to pay off the firm’s debts. The funds were repaid within 2 weeks before any money was due to be paid so no client was affected. Which of the following best describes the professional conduct implications of these actions?
options: No breaches of the conduct regulations have occurred as the COFA and the solicitor acted in the best interests of the clients in the long run by safeguarding the short-term future of the firm by paying using client money to pay its debts.
No breaches have occurred as the COFA is responsible for deciding what satisfies the regulations.
The COFA has breached conduct regulations by making the appointment and using the funds for the purposes of the firm.
No breaches of the conduct regulations have occurred as the money was repaid and no harm was caused to the firm’s clients.
The COFA and the solicitor have breached the conduct regulations by making the appointment and diverting the client funds for the use of the firm.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is the compliance officer for legal practice (COLP) of a medium- sized firm. The firm recruits a new solicitor to expand its conveyancing team. After the interviews, one candidate is selected for appointment. The successful recruit provides a utility bill as proof of address, an expired passport, and a copy of their practising certificate from the year before as part of the recruitment process. The COLP is satisfied that the documents are sufficient proof of identity and competence, and does not seek any references or verification from the SRA. A few months later, the new solicitor diverts funds paid by a client to fund a property purchase. It turns out that the documents provided as part of the recruitment process were all forged, and the applicant had in fact been banned from practising by the SRA on account of fraud. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications of the COLP’s actions?
options: The COLP has not breached any conduct regulations as it is incumbent upon the firm to establish recruitment procedures and follow them.
The COLP has acted appropriately as there were no reasonable grounds to suspect that the applicant was not who they said they were.
The solicitor has breached conduct regulations by failing to act with competence.
The COLP has breached conduct regulations by failing to act with integrity.
The COLP has breached conduct regulations by recruiting an individual who had been banned by the SRA.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is acting for a defendant in a personal injury matter. The case is settled on the basis that the defendant will pay damages of £10,000. The solicitor undertakes that the £10,000 will be paid within 7 days. The firm’s policy is that when an undertaking is given, a written note must be placed on the client’s file. The solicitor puts a written note on the file and then goes on a 2-week holiday. No one from the firm looks at the file in the solicitor’s absence and consequently the £10,000 is not paid on the due date. Which of the following best describes who has breached the Code of Conduct?
options: The solicitor is not in breach of the Code of Conduct because they have complied with firm’s policy.
The solicitor, the firm and the COLP are all in breach of the Code of Conduct.
As the person who gave the undertaking, the solicitor alone has breached the Code of Conduct.
The firm’s managers bear ultimate responsibility and so they alone have breached the Code.
The firm’s COLP bears ultimate responsibility and so they alone have breached the Code.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is the managing partner of a medium-sized high street law firm specialising in family law. A junior solicitor of the firm represents a client in an acrimonious divorce in which the client is ordered to give their spouse half of the family assets. The client is outraged and blames the firm for failing to robustly defend their interests in the proceedings. The client makes a formal complaint to the partner claiming that the solicitor who represented them was negligent, incompetent, and rude. The partner reads the complaint and “dismisses” it as baseless without speaking to the solicitor in question or the client. The firm’s complaints procedure requires a formal inquiry into all complaints. The client is not satisfied and wishes to escalate matters, but the partner tells them that the matter is “closed”, and they should move on. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the professional conduct implications in the scenario?
options: The solicitor, as managing partner, has the mandate to resolve all client complaints as they deem fit.

The firm has breached its professional conduct obligations by failing to deal with the complaint in line with its internal procedures and informing the client of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman and the SRA.
The firm has breached the professional conduct regulations by failing to deal with the matter in accordance with the internal procedures in place.
There are no conduct implications if the firm has an internal complaints procedure, and it has been followed.
The firm is obliged to inform the client of their right to make a complaint to the Legal Ombudsman and the SRA in the event that they are not satisfied with the service provided.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor acts for a client wishing to buy a detox camp business. Although the client is happy with the purchase, the solicitor has not fully read the contract until after the sale and discovers that there is a clause in the fine print that will entitle the vendor to free treatments for the rest of their life. The solicitor approaches the vendor and convinces them not to enforce the clause. The vendor agrees not to enforce the clause in exchange for a one-off sum of £3,000. The solicitor pays the vendor and passes on this cost to the client as a miscellaneous item on the cost of acting for them. The client does not dispute this and pays the sum without being informed of the real purpose of the payment. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications of the solicitor’s actions?
options: There are no professional conduct implications as the solicitor has not personally profited from the transaction.
The solicitor has acted dishonestly in handling the matter.
There are no professional conduct implications as the client has achieved their purpose.
There are no professional conduct implications as the solicitor has acted in the best interests of client.
The solicitor has breached the professional conduct regulations by not informing the client of their poor handling of the matter and the potential claim they may have against them.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A firm of solicitors dismisses a senior partner on the grounds of gross misconduct involving financial impropriety. Unknown to the firm, the senior partner downloads confidential information relating to some of the firm’s clients including details of addresses, legal matters handled as well as financial affairs. As revenge for the termination of employment, the former senior partner uploads all the information on their private social media accounts. Some of the information uploaded goes viral around the world. The firm can have the information removed from the social media sites after 48 hours. The former senior partner is facing criminal prosecution regarding the misuse of the information. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications in the circumstances?
options: The firm has breached its duty to act in the best interests of the clients.
The firm has breached its professional conduct obligation to maintain client confidentiality.
There are no professional conduct implications as the senior partner no longer works for the firm and cannot be said to be acting for the firm.
There are no professional conduct implications because the firm acted very quickly to have the information removed from the social media sites.
There are no professional conduct implications since there is an ongoing criminal prosecution.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A staff member in a large firm of solicitors steals money from a client account. The firm makes good the loss, dismisses the staff member, informs the police and puts in place procedures to ensure that the situation does not arise again. Should the matter still be reported to the SRA?
options: Yes, there is a need to report this to the SRA although it does not amount to a material breach.
Yes, there is a need for the firm’s compliance officer to record the incident and report it to the SRA as this amounts to a material breach.
Yes, there is a need for the firm’s compliance officer to record the incident and report it to the Legal Ombudsman as this amounts to a material breach.
The obligation to report is that of the most senior partner in the firm.
The firm has taken all the necessary steps required to remedy the breach and no further reporting obligations will be required.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A new client instructs a fee earner on a negligence claim. At the initial meeting with the client and in the client care letter, the fee earner fails to notify the client of their right to complain. The fee earner later notifies the client upon realising their omission (without prompting from the client). This is the first time the fee earner has done this. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications for the firm’s compliance officer for legal practice (COLP)?
options: This is the first time this has happened, and the error has been corrected without any loss to the client. Accordingly, there are no conduct obligations on the COLP.
There is a duty on the COLP to record and report, regardless of whether this amounts to a serious breach or not.
There are no professional conduct obligations on the COLP. Any obligation to report would be for the fee earner personally.
There will be no duty on the COLP to record and report as this does not amount to a serious breach.
The COLP has breached conduct regulations by recruiting a fee earner who is clearly incompetent.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is the sole partner of a small firm specialising in family law. The solicitor is acting for a client in a divorce, which is particularly acrimonious as one spouse alleges violence by the other and are living in a domestic violence shelter. The solicitor asks a junior solicitor to file a medical report in the matter with the court ensuring that details of the client’s address are redacted. The junior solicitor who is new to the firm instead attaches the document to a bulk email they are drafting to send to all of the firm’s clients. The junior solicitor does not realise the mistake and sends the document to all clients and only realises the error when clients call the firm to inform them of what has happened. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications of the junior solicitor’s action?
options: The firm has breached its professional conduct obligations as it owes a duty to the client but the solicitors have not breached their professional conduct obligations.
The sole partner is responsible for the conduct of the firm and has breached the professional conduct regulations.
The sole partner, the junior solicitor and the firm have breached the professional conduct regulations by disclosing confidential information of the client.
The firm and the junior solicitor have breached professional conduct regulations, but the sole partner has not breached any conduct regulations.
There are no professional conduct obligations, unless the client has suffered harm or the information has been misused.
questions.subject: Ethics and Professional Conduct
questions.source: COND3.4: Code of Conduct for firms: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A car owner puts a sign on their car outside their house saying “For Sale £5,000 or nearest offer. Only 40,000 miles and 10 months MOT”. A prospective buyer knocks on the owner’s door and says they will pay the £5,000, but the owner of the car has just been online and realised they could get more on “We Buy Any Car”, so they are no longer prepared to sell for £5,000. The prospective buyer insists there is a binding contract to sell for £5,000. Is the prospective buyer correct?
options: No, because the owner revoked their offer.
No, because the sign on the car was only an invitation to treat, not an offer capable of acceptance.
Yes, because the sign was a unilateral offer and the prospective buyer accepted by performance.
Yes, because there was a clear offer and they accepted it.
No, because the owner is free to contract with whoever they wish.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A council puts a building contract for construction of a new leisure centre out to tender, specifying that the contract will go to the lowest bidder and that all bids must be submitted, with full plans, by 9am on the closing date. At 8am on the closing date, Contractor 1 submits a bid for £2 million, Contractor 2 submits a bid confirming that it will perform the contract for £100,000 less than any other bidder and Contractor 3 submits a bid of £1 million with no plans. At 10am on the closing date, Contractor 4 submits a bid of £1.2 million. Which contractor should be awarded the contract?
options: Contractor 1 because their bid gave an exact price and was submitted on time.
Contractor 3 because their bid was the lowest bid at an exact price and was submitted on time.
Contractor 4 because their bid was the lowest bid at an exact price and was only slightly late.
Contractor 2 because their bid was, effectively, the lowest bid and was submitted on time.
The council has complete discretion to choose which contractor to award the contract to, as the tender was only an invitation to treat.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A homeowner, who is moving from a house to a flat where they are not allowed pets, agrees to sell their pedigree French bulldog to their neighbour for £100, knowing that the neighbour is very fond of the dog and will give it a good home. However, on the day of the move the homeowner knocks on their neighbour’s door asking for more money as they found out the dog is worth over £1,000, so £100 is not a fair price. Is there a binding contract?
options: No, because this is an example of past consideration.
Yes, as consideration only has to be sufficient, not economically adequate.
No, because the homeowner has made a mistake.
No, because £100 is not adequate consideration when the dog is worth over £1000.
Yes, because the relevant factor is that the neighbour will give the dog a good home.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A teacher owed their friend £2,000. The friend was aware that the teacher was experiencing some financial difficulties and told the teacher that if they paid on time, they would only need to pay half the money. The teacher duly paid half the money on the date the friend had asked. When the teacher’s financial situation subsequently improved, the friend asked them to pay the other half of the money. Can the friend recover the balance?
options: No, because it was a social agreement and not legally enforceable.
No, the debt has been paid because the friend previously agreed to accept only half the money.
No, the debt has been paid because, by paying on time, the friend accepted the teacher’s contractual offer to vary the terms of their agreement.
Yes, because the value of the debt means that the commercial presumption will apply.
Yes, the debt has not been paid because it was not paid in full by the due date.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A wife, who is having trouble in their marriage to their husband, agrees to lend their husband £1,000 to go on holiday with friends. The wife is hoping that it will make their husband realise they miss them and it will reignite a spark within the marriage. Sadly, the holiday has the opposite effect, and the husband decides to start divorce proceedings. The wife asks the husband for the £1,000 back. The husband refuses, saying they were still owed a birthday present from the previous year anyway. Is the wife entitled to the money back?
options: No, because the person did not get the agreement to repay in writing.
Yes, because they are now getting divorced.
Yes, because the husband originally agreed that it was just a loan.
No, because they are married there is presumed to be no intention to create legal relations.
Yes, because the couple are experiencing trouble in their marriage, so the presumption of no intention to create legal relations is rebutted.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An interior designer borrowed £5,000 from their restaurateur cousin to assist in setting up an interior design business. In return, the interior designer agreed to repay the restaurateur as soon as possible and to assist them in redecorating the interior of one of their restaurants. When the restaurant opened there was a lot of favourable publicity, especially with regard to the new décor and business boomed. The interior designer’s business also benefited from being showcased in the restaurant. The interior designer now tells the restaurateur they consider the design work for the restaurant is equivalent to £5,000, so they do not intend to repay the loan. Can the restaurateur recover the money?
options: Yes, there is a claim because consideration has been provided.
Yes, there is a claim because this is not a social arrangement.
No, there is no claim because they are cousins.
No, there is no claim because this is a social arrangement.
No, there is no claim because the value of the work balances out.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A manufacturer of garden sheds and a supplier of timber agreed verbally with a supplier that the supplier would supply it with the “most optimum timber available at the going rate”. Two weeks later, the manufacturer requested an initial quantity of timber from the supplier, but the supplier advised it was unable to supply any timber to the manufacturer, as the supplier had just agreed to an exclusivity deal with another garden shed manufacturer. What advice would you give to the manufacturer?
options: There is no contract as the “most optimum timber” is too vague.
The manufacturer can bring a claim for breach of contract against the supplier.
There is no contract because the supplier has agreed to enter into exclusivity with another customer.
There is a contract because the terms are usual in their type of industry.
There is no contract because there is no certainty on price.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A 17-year-old enters into a lease for a flat with a rent of £500 per calendar month. Their parents act as guarantors and when the teenager disappears after six months, owing £1,500 in rental arrears, the landlord seeks to recover the loss from the parents. What is the legal position?
options: The landlord cannot claim the arrears from the parents as the lease was not for the minor’s benefit.
The landlord can claim the money from the parents as a guarantee of a minor’s obligations is enforceable.
The landlord cannot claim the money from the parents as the 17-year- old minor did not have capacity to enter into the lease in the first place.
The landlord can only claim the arrears from the parents if they first use all reasonable endeavours to locate the minor and get the money from them.
The landlord cannot claim the rent as the minor has repudiated the contract within a reasonable time.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Upon a marriage, the bride and groom’s respective fathers agreed with each other to pay the happy couple an allowance of £5,000 per year for the first 10 years of their marriage. However, the bride’s father died three years after the wedding and his estate refused to carry on paying the allowance. Could the married couple claim against the estate of her deceased father?
options: Yes, as they had provided consideration by staying married.
No, as they were not party to the original contract.
No, as they had not provided any consideration for the original contract.
Yes, at common law as they were third parties who were intended to benefit under the contract.
Yes, under statute as they were third parties who were intended to benefit under the contract.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A politician has contracted with an agency, under which the agency provides a personal assistant to the politician on a rolling monthly basis. The personal assistant provided by the agency is offered a large sum of money by a newspaper to publish their memoirs when they finish working with the politician. The politician finds out and applies for an injunction, citing the confidentiality clause in the contract between the politician and the agency. Can the confidentiality clause be enforced against the personal assistant?
options: Yes, because it is a term of the contract.
Yes, using the rules relating to privity, the clause applies to the personal assistant.
No, because the personal assistant is not a party to the contract and not bound by it.
No, because it is anticipatory breach and could still be rectified.
No, because the personal assistant still works for the politician and has not published anything yet.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.1: Formation: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A shop owner orders some bread to sell in their delicatessen. They tell the baker it is vital the bread is made with organic flour as the delicatessen only sells organic products. The baker assures the shop owner they will only use organic flour. However, the written order document, as drawn up by the baker, does not specifically mention the word “organic”. What is the legal status of the requirement/specification?
options: It was a term incorporated through a course of dealing.
It was a term of the contract due to the expressed importance of the specification.
It was only a representation as it was not included in the written contract.
It was a term of the contract as it was stated just before the contract was finalised.
It was an implied term due to trade custom.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A famous opera singer misses the first night of a series of six concerts they are contracted to appear in, but says they are available for the other five nights. However, their failure to attend on the first night has impacted ticket sales for the remaining nights. The concert organiser refuses to pay the opera singer anything at all. What is the legal position?
options: The opera singer should be paid nothing at all, as attendance on the first night is fundamental and was a condition of the contract.
The opera singer should be paid for the remaining five nights as attendance on the first night was only a warranty of the contract.
The opera singer should be paid in full as they have substantially performed.
The opera singer should be paid nothing at all, as it was an implied term that attendance on the first night was required.
The opera singer should be paid nothing at all, as attendance on the first night was an innominate term, the consequences of the breach of which have been substantial.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A builder who is carrying out an extension to a property under a written contract agrees with the property owners to carry out some additional work in exchange for an old car that the owners have but are no longer using. Will this variation agreement be valid?
options: No, it is invalid. The contract cannot be varied, as it is subject to relevant consumer protection legislation.
It will only be a valid variation if it is evidenced in writing.
Yes, it is a valid variation to the contract by mutual agreement.
Yes, it is a valid variation to the contract by mutual agreement. It will only be a valid variation if the old car is of sufficient value.
No, it is invalid. The common law does not allow for variations to an initial contract.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A department store ordered boxed chocolates to sell in its store. It was listed as a written term of the contract that the chocolates be packaged in the store’s own-brand packaging, as the store famously only sells own- branded products. Once delivered it was discovered that the chocolates were instead in packaging representing the manufacturer’s brand. The manufacturer claims the packaging detail was only a warranty and the store can still sell the goods. The department store says it was obviously a condition and they cannot sell the goods. What is the likely legal position?
options: The clause will be held to be a warranty of the contract.
The clause will be held to be a condition of the contract.

The clause will be held to be a condition of the contract. The clause was an innominate term, the breach of which amounts to a breach of a warranty as it does not deprive the department store of the “substantial benefit” of the contract.
The clause was an innominate term, the breach of which amounts to a breach of a condition as it deprives the department store of the “substantial benefit” of the contract.
The promise to supply the chocolates in the store’s own-branded packaging was only a mere representation.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A joiner, who is a sole trader, entered a verbal contract for the purchase of second-hand tools from a large tool hire company. There were no specific express terms as to quality. The tools turned out to be faulty. What is the legal position?
options: There will be relevant statutory implied terms that apply to this business-to-business transaction.
There will only be relevant implied terms if they formed part of previous contracts entered into between these two parties.
There will only be implied terms if there is relevant trade custom.
There will be relevant terms that are routinely implied to tool-purchase contracts.
There will be relevant statutory implied terms that apply, as the sole trader qualifies as a consumer in this context.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A worker successfully applies for a job as an administrator for a construction company. In the prospective contract of employment, it states that the worker's usual place of work as “remote – homeworking”. However, there is a mobility clause which states that they can be required to work anywhere the company needs administrative support. When the worker asks about this clause, they are told, “Don't worry. Central admin never goes on- site”. The worker signs and returns the contract and has worked for the company for three years from home. The worker has just been told they will be working on-site 25 miles away for the next three weeks. They are not happy about this. Do they have any legal redress?
options: Yes, the statement about the effect of the mobility clause was an oral warranty and forms part of the contract. The worker does not have to go on-site.
Yes, the contract was written and contained an express term providing the working will work remotely, from home. The worker does not have to go on-site.
No, the statement about the effect of the mobility clause was a representation and does not form part of the contract. The worker must go on-site.
No, the contract was written and contained an express term as to mobility. The worker must go on-site.
No, the contract was written and was an entire agreement. The worker must go on-site.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A shop owner who sells vintage clothes takes their stock of vintage coats to a local dry cleaner. The coats are quite grubby, so the dry cleaner suggests they try a new experimental method of cleaning. The shop owner is a bit unsure so the dry cleaner offers the service at half price but says the usual exclusion clause within the dry cleaner’s standard terms of business will apply, whereby the dry cleaner will not be responsible for any loss or damage, “howsoever caused, including any loss or damage caused by negligence”. The cleaning method causes some of the older coats to disintegrate. Will the dry cleaner be able to rely on the exclusion clause?
options: Yes, the clause was reasonable because the shop owner received an inducement.
No, because the dry cleaner should have insured against the loss.
No, because it was a consumer contract.
Yes, as long as the dry cleaner was not negligent.
No, because there was a grossly disproportionate and unreasonable allocation of respective risks.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A building company contracted to carry out some work on a factory. During the work, the builders negligently injured the factory owner and caused damage to the factory. The owner is claiming damages of £5,000 for the injury and £20,000 for the damage to the factory. The builders are seeking to rely on their standard contractual terms, which include the following clauses: “(a) Liability for any personal injury is limited to £1,000 howsoever caused and (b) Liability for any damage to property is limited to £5,000 howsoever caused”. The builders had sent their standard terms to the owner after the particular contract was concluded. They had done the same on the 12 previous occasions they had contracted with the owner during the past five years. Can the building company rely on the limitation clause?
options: Partially. The limitation clause will be effective for the property damage only as it has been properly incorporated.
No, the limitation clause will fail as it is onerous and has not been drawn to the owner’s attention.
No, the limitation clause will fail as it is not a genuine pre-estimate of damages.
No, the limitation clause has not been incorporated into the contract, as the owner did not receive it until after the contract had been concluded.
Yes, the limitation clause will be effective for both personal injury and the property damage as it has been properly incorporated.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A couple rent a seaside holiday flat from a large lettings company. Their booking document states that the flat will be £150 per night. The couple do not notice some small, faint print at the bottom of the document which states that they will also be charged an additional £50 per night for use of all the fixtures, fittings and furniture. What is the likely legal status of this clause?
options: The clause will be binding as this is not a consumer contract.
The clause will not be binding as it is not transparent and prominent.
The clause will not be binding as it is not transparent and prominent. The clause will be subject to the test of reasonableness.
The clause will be binding as it is a core term and, as such, will be excluded from the scope of fairness under the relevant consumer legislation.
The clause will not be binding, as it is unfair under the relevant consumer legislation.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.2_ Contract terms_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A couple agreed to purchase an old sailing boat. Their intention was to sail around the world then write a book about their adventures. The couple concluded the purchase contract and handed over the money to the seller. However, unbeknownst to all parties the boat had sunk the day before the contract was agreed. What effect, if any, has the sinking of the boat on the contract?
options: The boat is central to the performance of the contract so the contract is discharged by breach.
The boat is central to the performance of the contract so the parties could agree to discharge the contract.
The boat is central to the performance of the contract so the contract is discharged by non-performance.
The boat is central to the performance of the contract so the contract is void for mistake.
The boat is central to the performance of the contract so the contract is discharged by frustration.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A purchaser agrees to buy a plot of land on the Yorkshire coast from a local landowner. Neither party realises that the plot no longer exists, as it was part of an area that fell into the sea, as a result of coastal erosion, the week before they entered into the contract. What is the legal position?
options: The contract will be void for common mistake.
The contract will be void for common mistake. The contract is valid and the purchaser will still have to pay for the land, as they did not make sufficient enquiries.
The contract will be void for unilateral mistake.
The purchaser can seek rescission of the contact due to the seller’s misrepresentation.
The contract will be void for mutual mistake.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A witness in a civil case entered a verbal contract with the claimant to say in court whatever the claimant wanted, in return for a substantial payment. However, on the day of the trial the witness failed to attend court. What is the legal position?
options: The contract is unenforceable, as it constitues duress.
The contract is enforceable and the claimant can claim damages against the witness for their failure to attend.
The contract is unenforceable for illegality.
The contract is unenforceable for illegality.

The contract was void as the witness was already under a legal duty to attend court and was not providing any further consideration for the payment. The contract is unenforceable as it was not evidenced in writing.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A purchaser wants to buy their neighbour’s car and tells them that, unless they sell it to them for £2,000, they will break their leg. The owner of the car knows the car is worth about £5,000 but is scared so agrees. A week later the owner changes their mind after the purchaser is arrested for assault. What is the legal position?
options: The contract will be set aside due to duress to the person.
The contract will be set aside due to duress to the person. The contract will not be set aside because it is valid.
The contract will be set aside for undue influence.
The contract will not be set aside as there was no threat made to the seller’s family.
The contract will be set aside for economic duress.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An aspiring stockbroker asks their independently wealthy spouse to stand surety for (that is, guarantee) debts they have incurred gambling on the stock exchange. The spouse initially refuses but the aspiring stockbroker says they will leave the spouse if they do not agree. The spouse goes ahead and acts as surety (without even meeting with the bank) until they find out, two weeks later, that the aspiring stockbroker has now run up debts in excess of £1 million. Is the spouse likely to have to pay this in full?
options: No. The bank creditor was put on notice of the possibility of undue influence when the spouse agreed to stand surety for the debt.
No, as the stockbroker was guilty of duress to the person.
It will depend on how wealthy they are.
Yes, as there was no actual undue influence.
Yes, as spouses and civil partners do not automatically raise the presumption of undue influence.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A purchaser wished to buy a painting by a famous and sought-after artist, who was a distant relative. They did not know much about art, but they knew what they liked when they saw it. The purchaser registered their interest with an art dealer who said they had a painting by the artist for sale. The purchaser asked if the painting was genuinely by the artist, making it clear they would not purchase unless it was by their relative. The art dealer took all reasonable steps to verify the painting and confirmed that it was genuine. The purchaser bought the painting for £8,000. Eighteen months ago, the purchaser discovered the painting was a very good forgery and worth about £150. When they bought the painting, works by the artist were selling for £20,000 and the price has remained stable. Ignoring interest, what is the amount of damages the purchaser can claim?
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A customer phoned a local dealer and explained that they wanted a cheap, reliable and economic car. It was very important to them that the car was as fuel efficient as possible. The dealer told them they had a second-hand Kia Rio in their price range that "would be just the ticket". The dealer said it was a "great little runner and will do 50mpg easily". The customer bought the car for £5,000 but after a few weeks found that it stalled a lot and was not doing more than 35mpg. The customer took it back to the dealer where they fixed the stalling fault. However, after another six months the car was not achieving more than 38mpg and was costing substantially more to run than the person budgeted for. Can the customer bring any action against the dealer?
options: Yes, because the dealer’s promise that the car was a “good little runner and will do 50mpg easily” is a contractual warranty.
Yes, because there is an actionable misrepresentation by describing the car as a "great little runner" when it was not reliable.
Yes, because there is an actionable misrepresentation by giving the miles per gallon as over 50mpg when it never achieves that.
No, because although there were actionable misrepresentations the person affirmed the contract by accepting the repairs and continuing to use the car.
No, because there is no evidence of an inducement.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A donor donated to a charity after being told by the treasurer that the charity had a good track record in successful nominations to the UK political honours committees. The treasurer told the donor that people like them would be a positive addition to the House of Lords. When the next honours list was published, the donor's name was not on it. The donor wants to get their money back from the charity. What would be the most likely outcome?
options: No contract because it is against public policy to be able to buy honours.
No contract because it is against public policy to be able to buy honours. No contract owing to a failure of consideration because the treasurer failed to carry out their promise.
A successful action in misrepresentation for the statement by the treasurer about being able to influence the award of honours.
No contract as there was a complete failure of performance so the person could repudiate and claim damages.
No contract because the agreement was not in writing and certain types of contract must be in writing.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A developer wishing to build a new shopping centre needs to buy a small terrace of three houses to clear the site. The developer approaches the homeowners with an offer and two of them accept. The third homeowner rejects the offer, saying the only way they are leaving the house is “in a pine box”. The developer says, “If that is what it takes, it can be arranged”. The developer tells the homeowner they have a week to think about it. When the developer returns the resident says they do not have much of an option so they will take the money and they sign a written agreement to this effect. Two months after the sale, the homeowner discovers the development is not going ahead as the council have revoked planning permission. The houses are still standing. The homeowner wishes to return to their former home. What is the likely outcome in contract?
options: The homeowner was not subject to duress over the sale because the developer presented a credible alternative option in the form of the developer’s original offer.
The resident was subject to duress over the sale. The contract is void.
The resident can elect to have the contract set aside.
The resident can elect to have the contract set aside. The person was subject to duress over the sale but there is a lapse of time that will bar them from claiming.
The homeowner was not subject to duress over the sale. Their only option is to try to buy the house back from the developer.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A first-time church attender was so struck by the message, they decided to formally join the church as a member. The minister explained that the church asked for a "faith commitment" from its members. In addition to giving money, members were expected to work for the church in their homeless hostel and their behaviour was closely controlled. The church attender had an inheritance of £100,000. They decided to give £20,000 to the church immediately and changed their will to leave the rest to the church. The church attender worked for the church until they became ill and were taken home by their parents to recuperate. After several years away from the church, the church attender decided they needed a proper job and a place of their own. They changed their will and asked for their money back. Will the church have to return the money?
options: No, there was presumed influence under a protected relationship. The person's gift was not valid. However, lapse of time means rescission is not possible.
No, there was no actual undue influence. The gift was valid.
No, there was actual undue influence. The person's gift was not valid. However, lapse of time means rescission is not possible.
Yes, there was actual undue influence. The person's gift was not valid.
Yes, there was presumed influence under a protected relationship. The person's gift was not valid.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.3_ Vitiating factors_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A homeowner contracted with a builder to carry out adaptations to their house to make it suitable for their disabled partner in the hope the partner would be discharged from hospital after a serious accident. The written contract contained an express term, which stated that work would begin on 1 May but only if it looked like the partner would be returning home in July. However, on 28 April, the partner died. What is the legal position?
options: The contract is discharged by a specified event.
The contract is discharged by a specified event. The contract is discharged by waiver.
The homeowner will be in breach of contract and will have to pay damages to the builder.
The contract is bilaterally discharged by agreement.
The contract is unilaterally discharged by agreement.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A homeowner books a caterer to provide food for their 40th birthday party, which is being held in their garden. A week before the party the homeowner receives a call from the caterer. The caterer says they will not be able to honour the contract as they are double-booked. The homeowner says they are not happy about this and still expect the caterer to attend. The homeowner then slams the phone down. The homeowner is so angry they decide to cater for the party themselves, with the help of friends. On the day of the party, the caterer does actually show up ready to cater for the party. The homeowner tells them to go away and says they will not pay them anything and will be suing for damages for all the stress they have caused. What is the legal position?
options: Neither party will have to pay anything as the homeowner accepted the caterer’s anticipatory breach and the contract was discharged.
The homeowner will have to pay the caterer in full as they chose to affirm the contract.
The homeowner will be able to claim some damages, but not including stress, due to the caterer’s anticipatory breach.
The person will have to pay the caterer 50% of the original price due to both parties being in breach.
The homeowner will be able to claim damages, including for stress, due to the caterer’s anticipatory breach.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A restaurant owner contracted with a decorator to redecorate their restaurant for a flat fee of £5,000. When the work was half finished, the restaurant was closed for several months due to a pandemic lockdown and only key workers were allowed to work. There was no way of knowing if or when the decorator would be able to resume the work. The restaurant owner refused to pay the decorator any money, claiming that the contract had been frustrated. What is the legal position?
options: The contract has been frustrated but the restaurant owner will likely have to pay the decorator a proportion of the fee.
The contract has been frustrated and the decorator will not be entitled to any payment.
The restaurant owner will have to pay the decorator the full amount as there has been substantial performance.
The contract has not been frustrated and the restaurant owner will have to pay the decorator the full amount.
The restaurant owner will be in breach of contract.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A plumber agrees to replace all the radiators in a house for £4,000. After the radiators in the kitchen and bathroom have been replaced, the owner decides they do not need the rest of the radiators replaced, as there is actually nothing wrong with them. The owner only wanted to change them for something more pleasing to look at and they have since discovered that the same outcome could be achieved for a much lower cost by simply buying radiator covers. The plumber has a full diary for the next six months and agrees to cease work on the basis that the owner pays £1,500 to reflect the value of the work completed to date. Which of the following best describes the legal position?
options: The parties had agreed to discharge the contract and the price to pay was £1,500.
The contract was for £4,000 and must be paid in full because the owner prevented performance.
The parties had agreed to vary the contract and the price to pay was £1,500.
The contract was for £4,000 but the plumber can claim £1,500 as quantum meruit for the work done.
The contract was for £4,000 and must be paid in full because the owner breached it.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A manufacturer makes environmentally friendly cars. The manufacturer enters into a five-year contract to supply cars to a car dealer. The dealer places an initial order for 1,500 cars to be delivered within 12 months. The order is accepted. Two weeks after the successful launch of the car, the manufacturer writes to the dealer stating that owing to production difficulties they will only be able to deliver 300 cars within the next 12 months. What is the legal position?
options: The breach of contract goes to the root of the contract so the dealer can repudiate.
The breach of contract does not deprive the dealer of the substantial benefit of the contract so the dealer cannot repudiate.
The number of cars is a condition precedent so the dealer can repudiate.
The breach of contract does not go to the root of the contract so the dealer cannot repudiate.
The breach is anticipatory so the dealer must wait for the date of delivery before bringing an action.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A bride lost one of a pair of unique, hand-crafted earrings. They wished to wear the earrings as part of their wedding outfit. The earrings had great sentimental value, as they were a present from the bride's grandparent on their 18th birthday. The bride contacted a jeweller, whose reputation rested on the production of exclusive handmade individual jewellery, to see if they could make a replacement. The bride was told that if they sent the earring the jeweller would try to make another to match it. The bride did so, enclosing a note saying “Thank you for agreeing to make an identical earring to match that which is enclosed. Please invoice me on completion." Unfortunately, when the earrings arrived, they did not match each other, and the bride felt they could not wear them for their wedding. Can the bride repudiate the contract?
options: No, because it is not possible in English contract law to claim damages for mere disappointment.
Yes, because the breach of contract deprives the bride of the substantial benefit of the contract.
Yes, because the breach of contract goes to the root of the contract.
Yes, because the breach of contract goes to the root of the contract. No, because the breach of contract does not go to the root of the contract.
No, because the breach of contract does not deprive the bride of the substantial benefit of the contract.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A company tendered for and obtained a contract to build an exclusive development of "mock Tudor executive style houses". The contract was valued at £200 million. Site clearance work commenced, and the company acquired the materials and the equipment necessary to complete the project within the 18-month time limit. After one week of clearance work, a bone was found and sent for examination. It was identified as an extremely rare Elaphrosaur neck bone. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) have placed a six-month nature conservation order on the site to allow excavation. The company wish to terminate the contract. Do they have grounds?
options: Yes, the delay to the contract will mean there is a breach of condition to complete within 18 months.
Yes, the order by the DCMS frustrates the contract.
No, the order by the DCMS does not frustrate the contract.
No, the order by the DCMS does not frustrate the contract. No, late performance is still good performance.
Yes, performance has been prevented owing to the order by the DCMS.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A decorator enters a contract with a homeowner to redecorate their flat. The contract price is £2,000 and a deposit of £500 was paid to the decorator on the day the contract was made. The decorator spends two days removing woodchip wallpaper from the walls and the ceilings. At the end of the second day the homeowner says: "I’ve changed my mind and will do the work myself. I’d like my money back please". What can the decorator recover at common law?
options: The homeowner has prevented the decorator from performing the contract and should pay the decorator on a quantum meruit basis.
The decorator can claim damages for loss of a chance to complete the work and recover the balance of the fee.
The decorator can affirm the contract and turn up to complete the job and claim the fee.
The decorator can claim for the breach of contract by the homeowner and recover the fee for the whole contract in expectation loss.
The homeowner has repudiated the contract and their liability is at an end.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A painter enters a contract with a homeowner to paint their flat. The contract price is £3,000 and a deposit of £600 was paid to the painter on the day the contract was made. The painter spends the first day stripping off all the old paint. The painter is then offered a more lucrative job elsewhere and abandons the current job. The homeowner is obliged to find an alternative painter to finish the work. Which of the following options best describes the legal position?
options: The homeowner does not have to pay on a quantum meruit basis for the work as it is only partial performance.
It was a divisible contract so the homeowner should pay for the work done.
The homeowner is liable to pay the painter on a quantum meruit basis for the work done.
The homeowner will have restitution for the payment already made.
This is an anticipatory breach situation. The homeowner should have waited to see if the painter came back.
questions.subject: Contract Law
questions.source: CONT1.4_ Termination_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

crml5.1.stem: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been accused of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and the alleged victim has ended up with a bruised eye after a particular incident occurred. Which of the following situations would stop the defendant from being guilty of the offence?
options: The defendant was running on ice realising it was a bit dangerous to do so and slipped and crashed into the victim, hitting the victim in the face and causing the bruise in the process.
The defendant slapped the victim causing them to slip on ice and hit a post causing the bruise.
The defendant was aiming a punch at someone but missed them and hit the victim in the face instead.
The defendant slapped the victim without realising how strong the blow was and the blow caused the bruise.
The defendant slapped the victim in the face. The blow was not very strong but the victim has a particular vulnerability to bruising.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has accidentally set fire to a mattress in a room where they and a victim are sleeping. The person notices the fire and leaves the room realising that there is a risk that the victim will get burnt. The victim does get severely burnt. Could the person be guilty of inflicting grievous bodily harm on the victim?
options: No, because the person did not intend to cause grievous bodily harm.
No, because the harm has not been inflicted by the person.
Yes, because there is a duty to prevent harm to others.
Yes, because the person created a dangerous situation and has caused a harm that results by not taking steps to remedy the situation.
No, because severe burns cannot be grievous bodily harm.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person is employed as a safety manager at an alleged victim’s company. The safety manager is currently subject to disciplinary proceedings, which they are very upset about. As a result, they do not tell the victim about a defective machine that they had spotted in the factory. The safety manager does not do so even though they see the victim checking the machine and they realise it is about to break and could injure the victim. The machine does break, causing the victim a significant gash. Has the person wounded the victim?
options: Yes, if the person’s contract required that they prevent harm to others.
No, because saying nothing to the victim about the machine is not “wounding”.
No, because the person has not taken an act that caused the wound.
No, because the person did not foresee a risk that the victim would be wounded.
Yes, because the person has created a dangerous situation.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been in a fight with victims A and B. The defendant stabbed at victim A, who dodged so that the knife wounded victim B. The defendant admits intending to hurt victim A seriously but claims only to have recognised a slight risk anyone else might get hurt. Can the defendant be guilty of wounding victim B with intent contrary to s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
options: No, because the defendant only foresaw a risk of harm to victim B rather than intending any harm.
No, because the defendant did not intend to cause victim B grievous bodily harm.
Yes, the defendant intended to create a risk of some harm to others.
Yes, because the defendant intended to cause victim A grievous bodily harm.
No, because victim A’s dodge was a break in the chain of causation.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is accused of inflicting grievous bodily harm on a victim. The victim has a serious psychiatric reaction to a campaign of harassment and silent intimidation by the defendant. In what circumstances can the defendant be guilty of an offence under s 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
