options: The defendant will only be guilty if the defendant realised that there was a risk of some harm to the victim at the start of the campaign of harassment.
The defendant can be guilty if the defendant realised there was a risk of some harm to the victim at some point during the campaign of harassment.
The defendant can be guilty because there is no requirement to foresee any harm so long as the defendant intended or was reckless as to an assault.
The defendant will only be guilty if the defendant had a specific duty not to prevent psychiatric harm to the defendant.
The defendant cannot be guilty because silence and intimidation is not “infliction”.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person is accused of having bumped into another passenger on a crowded train, causing annoyance. Could the person be guilty of battery?
options: Yes, if the person intended to inflict a particular level of physical force on the passenger or was reckless as to doing so.
No, because this is the sort of conduct that is ordinary incident of daily life so it is not unlawful.
Yes, if the person intended to inflict any level of physical force on the passenger.
No, because causing annoyance is not the mens rea of battery.
No, because the passenger is deemed to have consented to the risk of being bumped into when getting on a train.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant leaves a spring trap in a garden which is triggered by, and strikes, someone walking there. Has the defendant committed battery against the other person?
options: No, because it is not possible to commit battery indirectly by setting a trap.
Yes, but only if the defendant intended that someone would be struck by it.
Yes, but only if the defendant realised that there was a risk that the particular person might be struck by it or intended the particular person to be struck by it.
Yes, but only if the defendant realised that there was a risk that the particular person might be struck by it.
Yes, but only if the defendant realised that there was a risk that someone might be struck by it or intended for someone to be struck by it.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is accused of committing an assault. The victim heard the defendant shouting across a busy road, “Just you wait, you’ve got it coming,” while shaking a clenched fist at the victim. Could this constitute an assault?
options: Yes, if the defendant intended to inflict immediate unlawful physical force (or was reckless as to doing so).
No, because the defendant would not be able to carry out the threat immediately.
No, because the words show the defendant did not intend (and was not reckless as to) the immediate infliction of physical force.
No, because the words shouted negate any immediate force.
Yes, if the defendant intended to cause the other person to anticipate the infliction of immediate unlawful physical force (or was reckless as to doing so).
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A victim has received a number of silent phone calls that have been traced to the defendant and the defendant has been seen peering through the victim’s windows late at night. Are any of these actions assaults?
options: Only the silent calls can amount to an assault, and only then if the defendant is proven to have intended to cause (or was reckless as to causing) the apprehension of immediate unlawful physical force.
Both can be if the defendant intended to cause (or was reckless as to causing) the apprehension of immediate unlawful physical force.
Neither can be an assault unless it is proven that unlawful physical force could actually be inflicted immediately.
Only the lurking can be an assault and, only then if the defendant intended to cause (or was reckless as to causing) the apprehension of immediate unlawful physical force.
Neither can be an assault because neither suggest to the woman that unlawful physical force will be inflicted immediately.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant has been arrested because he was caught waving an unloaded gun at the victim, who was giving an interview on the merits of legalising gun ownership. The victim did not notice the incident and carried on giving the interview. The defendant says he knew the gun was not loaded but merely wanted to point the gun at the victim to show what being threatened with a gun was like. What prevents this from being an assault?
options: There was no apprehension by the victim.
There was no intention to carry out the threat.
The threat could not be carried out.
The man did not say anything threatening.
The victim was not frightened.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.1: Understanding and analysing criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crml5.2.stem: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant throws a stone at a victim wanting to hurt them but misses and breaks a window of the victim’s house. Could the defendant be guilty of criminal damage in such circumstances?
options: Yes, if the defendant realised there was a risk of missing and damaging the window.
No, because the defendant’s mens rea was directed at the victim and cannot be transferred to a window.
No, because the defendant did not want to damage the window in this instance.
Yes, because throwing stones can be regarded as a reckless action.
Yes, if the risk of missing and damaging the window was obvious.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for murder. The prosecution case is that the victim (a security guard) died in a factory fire that the defendant started for the sake of making a false insurance claim. The defendant admits starting the fire but denies having wanted to kill the victim, which the prosecution accepts. How must the judge direct the jury in relation to the mens rea for murder in a situation like this?
options: They must find the mens rea proven if they are sure that death or serious harm was virtually certain
They must find the mens rea proven if they are sure that death or serious harm was virtually certain and that the defendant realised that it was.
They may find the mens rea proven if they are sure that death or serious harm was virtually certain.
They may find the mens rea proven if they are sure that the defendant realised there was a risk of death or serious harm and it was, in fact, virtually certain.
They may find the mens rea proven if they are sure that death or serious harm was virtually certain, and that the defendant realised that it was.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for aggravated criminal damage, having tampered with electricity wires to divert electricity from a neighbour’s house in a way that the prosecution alleges has endangered life. The prosecution accepts that the defendant did not intend to endanger life. What must the jury decide in order to determine whether the defendant was reckless as to endangering life?
options: That it was obvious to the defendant that life would be endangered by the tampering but the defendant went on to take the risk unnecessarily anyway.
That it would be obvious to a reasonable person with the defendant’s knowledge of the situation that life would be endangered by the tampering.
That the defendant realised that life might be endangered by the tampering and that there was no good reason for doing it.
That it would be obvious to a reasonable person that life would be endangered by the tampering.
That the defendant realised that life might be endangered by the tampering but went on to take the risk unnecessarily anyway.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for criminal damage. The prosecution case is that the defendant, who was renting a property, damaged the flat by removing wall brackets on which a TV was fixed, ruining them in the process. The defendant claims not to have committed the offence because both the wall brackets and the TV were bought by the defendant. Will the defendant be guilty of criminal damage in such a situation?
options: Yes, if the prosecution prove that the defendant realised that the wall brackets might no longer belong to them.
No, because land (and therefore things attached to land) cannot be subject to criminal damage.
Yes, if the prosecution prove that the defendant intended to diminish the value of the rented property by doing so.
Yes, because the wall brackets would have ceased to belong to the defendant when fixed to the wall.
No, because there has been no damage to the wall within the property.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is charged with criminal damage, having nailed protest signs over advertising hoardings planted in the ground around a development site owned by a development company. Is it likely that the defendant’s actions will be found to amount to criminal damage?
options: No, because nothing has been taken from the hoarding and the hoarding is still functional and intact.
Yes, because the development company would have to remove the flags to gain the value of the hoardings.
No, because it could be easily remedied at no great cost or inconvenience.
Yes, because it negatively impacts on the value of the advertising at the property.
No, because the impact on the value of the hoarding itself would be minimal.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person is accused of setting fire to their own car during a dispute with his ex-partner. The person did so because he did not want their ex- partner to get ownership of it in a divorce settlement. The person has been charged with basic arson contrary to s 1(3) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971. Has the man committed criminal damage to the car?
options: Yes, if setting fire to the car endangered the lives of others.
Yes, if the partner had a share in the car at the time of the incident.
No, because it is not possible to be guilty of criminally damaging one’s own property.
Yes, if the partner had a share in the car and the man realised that this might be the case.
Yes, because it does not matter whether the property belonged to another person if the damage is caused by fire.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for aggravated criminal damage having damaged a lorry belonging to the defendant for the purposes of insurance fraud. Assuming that the damage is shown to be intentional, in what circumstances can the defendant be found guilty of the offence?
options: If it is proven that the defendant realised that the lorry belonged to another and that the lives of others might be endangered by the damage.
If it is proven that the defendant realised that the lives of others might be endangered by the damage.
If it is proven that the lives of others were endangered by the damage and the defendant realised that this might happen.
If it is proven that the lorry belonged to another, that lives of others were endangered by the damage and that the defendant realised these facts.
If it is proven that the defendant intended the lives of others to be endangered by the damage.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: During a rally, the defendant fires off a gun. The shot shatters a window and narrowly misses a person standing beyond it. The defendant denies having intended to put anyone’s life at risk claiming instead simply to have been joining in the spirit of the protest. Could the defendant be guilty of aggravated criminal damage?
options: Yes, if the defendant realised that firing the bullet through the window put the person in danger.
Yes, because the person’s life was put in danger by being shot at.
No, because there does not appear to be any recklessness as to endangering life by damage to property.
Yes, because firing a bullet through the window endangered the person.
No, because the person’s life was not in fact put in danger because the shot missed.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person was asked by a friend to retrieve a car that was part of a crash nearby. The person goes to the site, sees two cars (both undriveable due to the crash) and starts pulling the door off one of them in order to get inside so that they can tow it back to their friend’s house. As they are doing so a bystander arrives and tells the person it is the bystander’s car that they are taking the door off. The other car belongs to the person’s friend. In this situation is the man likely to have committed criminal damage?
options: No, because the cars are already so significantly damaged that what was done would not reduce their utility or value.
Yes, but only if the person made an unreasonable mistake about which car to take the door off.
No, because the person seems to have a genuine belief that what they were doing was consented to.
No, because they did not intend to damage a car belonging to that bystander and had no reason to believe it was her car.
Yes, because they deliberately damaged the car knowing it belonged to someone else.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor acts for a client who is charged with arson. The client tells a friend to give a false alibi that they were together at the friend’s home address on the date and time of the offence. The client informs the solicitor of this and instructs the solicitor to prepare and submit a witness statement to that effect. Which statement best reflects what the solicitor should do?
options: The solicitor should refuse to prepare and disclose the witness statement because to submit such evidence would amount to professional embarrassment for the solicitor’s firm.
The solicitor should explain their duty to the court and to others to the client and why such a statement cannot be put before the court, but then proceed on the basis of the client’s instructions.
The solicitor should prepare and disclose the witness statement because the solicitor’s duty to act in the best interests of the client outweighs all other considerations.
The solicitor should refuse to prepare and disclose the witness statement because to submit such a statement would not be deemed as acting with independence.
The solicitor should refuse to prepare and disclose the witness statement because to submit such evidence would be misleading the court.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.2: Understanding fault and blame: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crml5.3.stem: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is charged with aggravated arson having set fire to rubbish piled up outside their own flat in a block of flats. The defendant was drunk at the time and said, while doing so “See this, it is a fire hazard and people might die if it catches fire,” at which point the defendant set the rubbish on fire. The defendant denies having intended to put any lives in danger and says that the offence was committed in a moment of drunken rage about the failure to collect rubbish. Can the defendant be convicted of aggravated arson on these facts?
options: No, because the defendant was reckless but lacked intent due to intoxication.
Yes, because the defendant seems to have foreseen the risk that lives could be endangered.
No, because the defendant’s discarded rubbish is not property belonging to another.
No, because the offence is one of specific intent.
Yes, because the offence is one of basic intent.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person is being prosecuted for causing grievous bodily harm, with intent to cause grievous bodily harm contrary to s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 but denies having intended any such harm because they were too drunk to think clearly after spending a number of hours drinking with friends. How should the jury be directed in relation to the defendant?
options: They should ignore the person’s intoxication because they were voluntarily intoxicated.
If the person did not intend to cause serious harm, they may convict the person of s 20 GBH whether or not the person realised some harm might occur.
If the person did not intend to cause serious harm, they must acquit the person of the s 18 offence.
If the person did not intend to cause serious harm, the jury may convict the person of s 20 GBH if the person realised that some harm might occur.
They must acquit the person because this is a crime of specific intent.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is accused of murder, having repeatedly punched the victim during a fight. The defendant claims to have been delirious due to the effects of taking a double dose of medication they had been prescribed and, for that reason, not to have realised that their actions would result in the victim’s death or serious injury. If the defendant's explanation is accepted, what offence are they most likely to be convicted of?
options: No offence, because there will be a lack of relevant mens rea.
Murder, because he was voluntarily intoxicated at the time of the attack.
Manslaughter, because he was involuntarily intoxicated at the time of the attack.
No offence, because he was involuntarily intoxicated at the time of the attack.
Manslaughter, because he was voluntarily intoxicated at the time of the attack.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is being prosecuted for wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and claims not to have realised what they were doing at the time because the victim had slipped a drug into their drink. Will the defendant be able to avoid conviction on this basis?
options: Only if they are able to prove they did not intend to cause grievous bodily harm.
Yes, unless the prosecution prove they in fact intended to cause grievous bodily harm.
Only if they are able to prove that the victim did slip the intoxicant into her drink.
No, because this is a crime of basic intent.
Yes, unless the prosecution prove that the victim did not slip the intoxicant into the defendant’s drink.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for murder and wishes to raise the defence of self-defence on the grounds that the victim attacked them while they were walking home. It is not clear on the evidence whether the victim was going to attack them, and the prosecution allege that the defendant irrationally assumed the victim was attacking them. Can the jury conclude that the defendant was acting in self-defence on this basis?
options: Not if the prosecution prove that they did not believe use of force was necessary or their use of force was unreasonable in the situation as they believed it to be.
Not if the prosecution prove that the use of force was not necessary or reasonable.
They can if the defence prove that the defendant believed that their use of force was necessary and reasonable.
They can if the defence prove that the defendant used necessary and reasonable force.
They can if the defence prove that the defendant believed use of force was necessary and that their use of force was reasonable in the situation as they believed it to be.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is on trial for inflicting grievous bodily harm, and claims that the injury to the victim happened when the defendant was running away from a third-party assailant and pushed the victim down some stairs to get past. Why might this defence be most likely to fail?
options: Because the defendant might not have reasonably believed the assailant posed a threat.
Because the injury was not proportionate to the threat.
Because the force used was not proportionate to the threat.
Because force was not used against the assailant.
Because it was not reasonable to use force in the circumstances.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is charged with manslaughter, having killed a person who was trying to take the defendant’s car in a public car park. The defendant is alleged to have hit the person repeatedly with a carjack even as the person was running away. Will the defendant be able to rely on self-defence in this case?
options: Yes, but only if it was reasonable to use force and the force used was proportionate.
No, because the victim was running away.
No, because the defendant hit the victim repeatedly.
Yes, but only if the force used was not grossly disproportionate to the threat as the defendant understood it.
Yes, but only if, based on the defendant’s perception of the situation, it was reasonable to use force and the force used was proportionate.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is on trial for shooting a man who, the defendant says, was threatening the defendant’s child. The fighting took place inside the victim’s house after the defendant went there to warn the victim off and the victim threatened to kill the child when they next saw them. Is the defendant likely to be able to rely on the defence of prevention of crime or defence of another in these circumstances?
options: Only if the use of force was not disproportionate to the threat that the defendant believed the victim posed.
Only if the use of force was not grossly disproportionate to the threat that the defendant believed the victim posed.
No, because the defendant had gone to the victim’s house.
No, because it is not likely to be reasonable to have used force in these circumstances.
Yes, because the victim was posing a significant threat to the child.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant has been prosecuted for murdering a victim the defendant found in their house. The victim was unarmed and turns out to be homeless and seems to have broken into the kitchen to steal some food. The defendant is alleged to have grabbed a sword and beaten the victim a number of times as the victim was trying to escape out the door. How should the jury decide whether the defendant was acting in self- defence in these circumstances?
options: They must decide whether the use of force was reasonable and may decide it was not if the force used was disproportionate but not grossly disproportionate.
They must decide whether the use of force was reasonable and may decide it was not if the force used was grossly disproportionate.
They must decide whether the use of force was proportionate.
They must decide whether the use of force was reasonable and must decide it was not if the force used was disproportionate.
They must decide whether the use of force was reasonable and may only decide it was not if the force used was grossly disproportionate.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is accused of murder and says, in evidence, that they got into such a rage when taunted by the victim about their mental illness that they could did not think about what they were doing and just lashed out with the pickaxe they were then holding. They wanted to hit the victim but did not think about what hitting them would do. The victim died from the wounds. Which offence is the man likely to have committed based on such an explanation?
options: Unlawful act manslaughter
Murder
Manslaughter by reason of loss of control
Assault occasioning actual bodily harm
Manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.3: Defences and their impact on criminal liability: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crml5.4.stem: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Defendant A is charged with criminal damage having convinced Defendant B to remove two fireplaces from a building owned by a victim. A told B that he owned the building. Which one of the following statements is true regarding whether A has committed criminal damage?
options: A will not be guilty because B will lack the mens rea for criminal damage.
A will be guilty as a principal if it is proven he caused B to cause the criminal damage and A intended damage and was reckless as to the property belonging to another.
A will not be guilty because B will have believed he had a lawful excuse for the damage.
A will be guilty as an accessory if it is proven that he intended to assist B commit the offence of criminal damage.
A cannot be guilty because B’s actions break the chain of causation between A’s acts and the ultimate damage.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Defendants A and B are alleged to have attacked a victim together and at the same time and the victim now has injuries that could amount to actual bodily harm. The victim remembers that both were punching and kicking them but cannot remember with certainty which injuries were inflicted by which of them. How will A and B be prosecuted?
options: Both can be prosecuted as co-principals and can potentially be found guilty of the offence.
The prosecution will have to choose one to be the principal and prosecute the other as an accessory.
Neither can be prosecuted because it will not be possible to show clearly which injuries were inflicted by which defendant.

Both can be prosecuted as co-principals but only one of them can be found guilty of the offence because only one can have “occasioned” ABH and will therefore have prevented the other defendant from doing so.
Both should be prosecuted as accessories and they can both be convicted if it can be shown that they were taking part in a joint enterprise.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is charged with murder of a victim as an accessory to a second defendant. There is evidence that the first defendant had suggested that the second kill the victim and that the first defendant wanted the victim dead but they have produced evidence that the second defendant had been talking about doing so anyway. Can the first defendant be an accessory to murder of the victim on this basis?
options: No, because the first defendant has not encouraged the second to do something as they were already going to do it.
Yes, if the first defendant intended to encourage the second to kill the victim and knew that what was said might do so.
Yes, if what the first defendant said made a difference to whether the second defendant would actually kill the victim and the first defendant realised it might do so.
Yes, if the first defendant realised that what was said might encourage the second defendant to kill the victim.
Yes, if what the first defendant said helped the second to kill the victim and the first defendant intended that it would do so.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Defendant A has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent to cause GBH on a victim and Defendant B is charged as an accessory. Both defendants were at a protest rally and the victim was a counter-protestor. Defendant A attacked the victim and Defendant B threw A a piece of wood with which A beat the victim. The defendants had never met each other before. Can Defendant B be convicted as an accessory to causing GBH with intent on the victim?
options: Yes, if Defendant B intended to cause Defendant A to use excessive force against the victim by use of the piece of wood.
Yes, if Defendant B intended to assist Defendant A to intentionally cause GBH on the victim and realised that Defendant A was not acting in self- defence.
Yes, if it is shown that Defendant B and Defendant A had previously discussed causing serious harm to counter-protesters.
No, because Defendant A and Defendant B do not know each other and have not planned the offence.
Yes, if Defendant B intended to assist Defendant A to intentionally cause some harm to the victim and realised that Defendant A was not acting in self-defence.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Defendant A is being prosecuted as an accessory to wounding a victim with intent contrary to s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The wound was caused by Defendant B using a knife that Defendant A had been told by B to leave by the back door of the restaurant where A is a cook. A knew that B is a significant figure in local gang crime but claims to have had no idea what the knife was going to be used for. Can Defendant A be convicted as an accessory to the wounding on these facts?
options: Yes, if Defendant A intended the knife to assist in the commission of an offence.
No, Defendant A does not have the intention to assist Defendant B to cause serious harm to the victim.
Yes, if Defendant A realised that the knife would assist Defendant B in committing a crime.
Yes, if Defendant A realised that the knife would assist someone in committing a crime.
No, because Defendant A does not know the person who is being assisted.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Defendant A is being prosecuted for murder of a victim. Defendants A and B were participating in a robbery. Defendant A held the victim down when B started punching them but B then pulled out a knife and stabbed the victim with it. Defendant A admits having intended to help B cause some harm to the victim but denies intending their death. What verdict should the jury return if they accept Defendant A’s explanation and conclude that B intended to kill the victim?
options: Murder because Defendant A was involved with an offence that led to death.
Unlawful act manslaughter because Defendant A did not intend serious harm but foresaw some harm and the victim died.
Murder because Defendant A intentionally assisted B’s killing of the victim.
Unlawful act manslaughter because Defendant A is an accomplice to B’s murder, which is an unlawful act that led to death.
Wounding because Defendant A intended some harm.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has hired someone to give her partner a “severe beating” having found out that the partner was having an affair. The hired person confronts the partner and asks for a bribe instead, but the partner reacts violently and the hired person kills the partner in reasonable self-defence. What can the defendant be convicted of?
options: Unlawful act manslaughter, as a principal, because the defendant encouraged a crime which caused death to the husband.
Causing GBH with intent, as an accessory, because the defendant encouraged the man to cause grievous bodily harm with the intention to cause such harm.
Murder, as an accessory, because the defendant encouraged the man to cause serious harm to the husband and the husband died.
No offence because the defendant has not encouraged the commission of an offence.
Murder, as a principal, because the defendant’s actions caused the death of her husband.
questions.subject: Criminal Liability
questions.source: CRML5.4_ Criminal liability for others and incomplete acts_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

crmp9.1.stem: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is attending a police station to represent a client and is concerned about how the client has been treated so far. Which of the following best represents what the solicitor should do to determine whether the police have been meeting their obligations to the client as a detainee?
options: Consult the Custody Record.
Ask the client to request a copy of the Custody Record on release from detention.
Ask the client.
Ask the investigating officer.
Ask the Custody Officer if the client has been treated well.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The Custody Record of a detainee shows they were put into a crowded cell with inadequate lighting and that at various points they were not provided with food and drink and did not gain adequate opportunities to sleep, all in breach of the duties for detention under Code C. During the detention the detainee confesses to the commission of an offence. How might will the failure of the police to comply with their Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 duties be best evidenced at trial?
options: By the investigating officers giving evidence.
By asking the Custody Officer if they can remember the circumstances of detention.
By the legal advisor giving evidence.
By referencing the Custody Record.
By the defendant giving evidence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has been arrested and detained on suspicion of criminal damage by daubing a £1,000 political advertising board with red paint (a summary offence). A police officer saw the person commit the offence and arrested them immediately. The person wishes to receive legal advice but a superintendent at the station has authorised a delay of legal advice on the basis that they have reasonable grounds for suspecting that exercising the right to legal advice will interfere with evidence. The detainee subsequently confesses during their Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 interview. The admissibility of the confession is challenged at trial. Which of the following is the best argument for the defence to exclude the confession?
options: The decision to delay legal advice confession can only be authorised by the Custody Officer.
This offence was summary only so there was no basis for preventing legal advice.
The decision to delay legal advice should have been made by an inspector.
There are no grounds ever for delaying access to legal advice to a suspect detained at a police station pending interview.
The requirement is that the superintendent must have reasonable grounds for believing, not merely suspecting, that exercising the right to legal advice will interfere with evidence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A man (the suspect) has been arrested for wounding with intent (an indictable-only offence) following a fight in a nightclub. The evidence from the witnesses is slightly contradictory as to whether the suspect might have been acting in self-defence. He has yet to be interviewed. The only comment the suspect made on arrest was to say, “I was just defending myself”. The Custody Officer is of the opinion that there is strong evidence that the suspect intentionally carried out the attack, that this was the cause of the victim’s wounds but that it is not clear at this point whether the attack was in self-defence. What decision can legitimately be made in relation to charging the suspect with s 18 wounding with intent at this point?
options: The Custody Officer cannot charge the suspect with s 18 wounding unless they decide that the evidence of self-defence is so weak that there is sufficient evidence to charge him.
The Custody Officer can refer the matter to an officer of the rank of at least superintendent for that officer to make a charging decision.
The Custody Officer can charge the suspect with s 18 wounding.
The Custody Officer must refer the matter to the Crown Prosecution Service for a charging decision.
The Custody Officer is not yet able to decide whether there is sufficient evidence to charge the suspect with an offence, given the doubts about whether he was acting in self-defence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has been arrested for an indictable offence and has been brought to a police station to be detained. Which of the following best reflects that which the Custody Officer is required to inform the person about?
options: That they have an immediate right to make a telephone call to a person known to them to tell them that they have been detained.
That they cannot be interviewed without a lawyer present.
The circumstances of the offence for which the person has been arrested.
That they are entitled to a copy of the custody record at any time.
How long they will be detained at the police station.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person was brought to a police station at 6pm and detained for questioning on suspicion of unlawful wounding (an indictable offence). The detention was lawfully and appropriately reviewed at 10.30pm. When should the next review of detention be conducted and by whom?
options: At 9.30am by an inspector (or higher ranked officer).
At 9am by an inspector (or higher ranked officer).
At 4.30am by a Custody Officer.
At 7.30am by an inspector (or higher ranked officer).
At 7.30am by a superintendent (or higher ranked officer).
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person has been (lawfully) detained in police custody since 2pm on Tuesday following their arrest for theft (an indictable offence). It is now 2pm on Wednesday. Which of the following statements best describes how continued detention can be lawfully authorised?
options: If the officer responsible for the station, who must be of at least the rank of superintendent, believes that it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or to obtain it through questioning.
If the magistrates’ court believes that it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or obtain it by questioning and that the investigation has been conducted “diligently and expeditiously”.
If the magistrates’ court believes that it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or obtain it by questioning.

If the officer responsible for the station (superintendent or above) believes that it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or to obtain it through questioning and that the investigation has been conducted “diligently and expeditiously”.
If an officer at, of least, the rank of inspector believes that it is necessary to secure or preserve evidence or to obtain it through questioning.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A police officer arrests a suspect, having seen him as a part of a crowd during an affray seemingly engaged in threatening unlawful violence. The suspect is taken to the police station to be detained. What reason could the officer provide to the custody officer for the arrest?
options: They suspected that the arrestee has committed an offence and suspected it was necessary.
They had reasonable grounds to believe that the arrestee has committed an indictable offence.
They had reasonable grounds to suspect that the arrestee has committed an offence and that they had reasonable grounds for believing the arrest to be necessary.
They believed that the arrestee has committed an arrestable offence.
They believed that an offence is about to be committed and suspects it would be for the best to arrest them.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: In the early hours of the morning, an officer discovers a suspect hiding in a bus shelter only 100 metres away from a shop that, only 30 minutes earlier, had been burgled. The officer notices that the suspect has cartons of cigarettes and a bottle of whiskey that may well have come from the shop and reasonably suspects that the suspect is the person responsible for the burglary. The officer asks the suspect to provide an explanation for having possession of these items. At this point, the suspect throws the cigarettes at the officer and runs away. The officer gives chase and grabs the suspect before restraining and handcuffing him. The suspect does not resist. What is the next most appropriate step that the officer should take in these circumstances?
options: The officer should advise the suspect following their arrest about their right to take legal advice and to have someone informed about their arrest.
The arresting officer should open a Custody Record at the scene to monitor detention.
The officer should caution the suspect despite it being impracticable to do so in these circumstances.
The officer should caution the suspect following the arrest, tell them the grounds for the arrest and take them to a police station.
The officer should caution the suspect following the arrest but need not tell them about the grounds for the arrest because they speak for themselves.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: At 5.30am on 4 July, a suspect is arrested in connection with an offence of wounding with intent and taken to the police station arriving at 6am, where a decision is made to detain. On their arrival at the police station, the original decision to detain is made by the custody sergeant who is not involved with the investigation. A review of the suspect’s detention is conducted by the custody officer at 12pm and 9pm. The suspect is provided with refreshments during their detention and breaks during the interview. It is now 4am on 5 July and the suspect is yet to be charged. It is only at this point that the suspect requests and consults a solicitor. What is the best advice the solicitor can give the suspect about their detention?
options: The detention should have been reviewed at 12pm, 9pm and next at 6am and those reviews and the original decision to detain should have been carried out by officers of higher rank.
The detention should have been reviewed at 12pm, 9pm and next at 6am by the Custody Officer.
The times of the reviews are correct, but those reviews should have been carried out by an officer of higher rank.
The detention did not need to be reviewed until the suspect had been at the police station for 24 hours.
The suspect has no legitimate grounds for complaint.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.1: At the police station – rights and processes: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crmp9.2.stem: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The police are investigating an attempted robbery that involved the use of a Ford Transit Van. There is no evidence that anyone other than the van driver was involved. They find the van in a different part of town and see a person walking away from it. Which statement most accurately reflects the police powers to question the person at this point?
options: They may question them under caution about the van if they have reasonable grounds for suspecting that they were involved in the offence.

They may question them not under caution to establish their identity and whether the van belongs to them. They are will not be able to ask them other any more questions other than at a police station.
They may question them not under caution to establish their identity and whether the van belongs to them. They are unlikely to be able to ask them any more questions other than at a police station.
They will have to take them to a police station to question them.
They may question them about the van if they arrest them and caution them first.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The police wish to interview a defendant following their arrest for three thefts from shops. They have been taken to an interview room. They are not accompanied by a legal advisor. What must the police do before interviewing the defendant?
options: They must remind the defendant of their entitlement to legal advice and ensure they have sufficient information about the alleged offences but there is no need for a caution, as this will have been given on arrest.

They must ensure the defendant has sufficient information about the alleged offences about which the defendant is being interviewed but the defendant will already have been told about legal advice when initially detained and cautioned on arrest.

They must remind the defendant that they are under caution and ensure they have sufficient information about the alleged offences not of their entitlement to legal advice, which will have been mentioned when they were detained.
They must remind the defendant that they are under caution and of their entitlement to legal advice and check that they understand why they were arrested.
They must remind the defendant that they are under caution and of their entitlement to legal advice and ensure they have sufficient information about the alleged offences to be interviewed.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A suspect is being interviewed in relation to a violent assault they are alleged to have committed on their partner. The suspect is being interviewed by a police sergeant. The suspect is represented by a qualified solicitor, who has advised them at the start of the interview not to answer any police questions. The police sergeant now wants to remove the solicitor from the interview. Which of the following best reflects the sergeant’s powers in this situation?
options: Because legal advice to remain silent and not to answer questions is not a basis for excluding a legal advisor from an interview, the sergeant cannot remove the solicitor from the interview.

Because there are grounds for believing the solicitor’s conduct and advice is hindering the investigation, the sergeant can obtain the authority of an officer of higher rank to remove the solicitor from the interview.
Because the defendant has a fundamental and unqualified right to legal advice from a qualified solicitor, the sergeant cannot remove the solicitor from the interview.

Because the sergeant believes that the solicitor’s advice prevents them from properly putting questions to the defendant, they can obtain the authority of an officer of higher rank to remove the solicitor from the interview.
Because the sergeant believes that the solicitor’s advice prevents them from properly putting questions to the defendant, they can remove the solicitor from the interview.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The police are about to interview a defendant at a police station about a number of fraud offences but the video recording facilities have broken. What is the best resolution the police have in relation to the recording of the interview from the alternatives below?
options: To wait until they are able to video record the interview.
Make an audio recording with an authorised recording device.
To make a written record of the interview if there is a concern about delay.
To take the defendant to another police station that has working recording facilities.
They must delay the interview until the facilities are repaired (which they must do as a matter of urgency).
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: remove the solicitor from the interview.
options: It is in their best interests to exercise their right to silence but there is a risk of adverse inferences being drawn against them at trial.
It is in their best interests to exercise their right to silence, as there is no risk of adverse inferences being drawn against them at trial because they relied on the solicitor’s advice.
It is in their best interests to exercise their right to silence until the police are willing to provide fuller information.
It is in their best interests to give full answers and to show co- operation with the police.
It is in their best interests to remain silent despite adverse inferences being drawn at trial and doing so is less risky at this point than answering questions without full information.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old youth in care is arrested for theft and detained at a police station. The defendant was arrested for shoplifting when out with her 19- year-old sister who was not involved with the offence. However, she appears to the Custody Officer to have a very poor understanding of what is happening. The Custody Officer wants to appoint an appropriate adult. The youth objects to her social worker being appointed and states she has little contact with her parents. She has requested that her elder sister take the role instead. Who would be most appropriate for the Custody Officer to appoint as the appropriate adult?
options: Another responsible adult independent of the police.
The older sister.
The social worker.
The defendant's solicitor.
The defendant's mother or father.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is arrested on a bridge over a dual carriageway. Police find the defendant in the process of throwing a concrete slab onto the road. The defendant is identified as one of two men who had been throwing slabs onto the road some time earlier. On arrest, the defendant is found with a plan of all the bridges on the carriageway and a mobile phone containing text messages to another person about the sabotaging of other locations. The defendant is taken to the police station and formally interviewed under caution with a solicitor present, who advises a no comment interview. The defendant declines to make any comment during interview, stating they have done so on legal advice. At trial, the defendant gives evidence, stating that he was acting under duress. Which of the following is the most accurate statement on the legal consequences of the defendant’s failure to comment?
options: It is possible for the court to draw an inference as appear proper if the court concludes the fact relied upon (duress) is one the defendant could reasonably have been expected to mention in interview.
It is not possible for the court to draw an adverse inference because there is a fundamental right to silence.
It is not possible to draw an adverse inference because he was acting on legal advice.
It is not possible to draw an adverse inference because no special caution was given.
It is possible to be convicted solely on the basis of an adverse inference alone because his silence proves him to be a discreditable witness.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A suspect is about to be interviewed about an arson attack on a shop owned by a business rival and is having a meeting with a solicitor. The suspect, who is married, says she was with her lover at the time of the alleged attack but does not want to mention this to protect the marriage. The solicitor is about to have a private consultation with the suspect and will need to advise on the possible future consequences if she fails to mention her alibi in interview but then relies upon it at trial. What is the best advice the solicitor can give the suspect on whether an adverse inference is likely to be drawn if the defendant does not disclose her defence in interview?
options: Failing to mention it means her guilt will be inferred because it is totally unreasonable for her not to have mentioned it.

Failing to mention the alibi in interview is preferable because the prosecution bears the burden of proving the case, so it is better to wait until trial to see whether there is enough reason to risk the marriage.

Failing to disclose you were elsewhere and with whom at the time of the arson are facts the suspect could quite reasonably have been expected to mention and an adverse inference may be drawn at trial.
Failing to mention it is sufficient on its own to find her guilty because it is totally unreasonable not to have mentioned it.

Failing to disclose you were with a lover at the time of the arson is a personal matter and, therefore, not a fact a person could reasonably have been expected to mention in interview and it would be improper to draw an adverse inference.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is on trial for grievous bodily harm with intent arising out of a fight outside a club. At the police station, he was not given the opportunity to consult a solicitor. During the police interview, he claimed that he was working at a shop at the time of the fight. During trial, the defendant admits under cross-examination not to have been working at the shop but rather to have been assisting in selling drugs elsewhere. How should the court deal the fact that the defendant has raised a new defence at trial?
options: An adverse inference cannot be drawn because the defendant has mentioned a fact (the drug deal) that could not reasonably have been mentioned during the police interview given the privilege against self- incrimination.
An adverse inference might be drawn because the defendant has mentioned a fact (the drug deal) that could reasonably have been mentioned during the police interview.
An adverse inference cannot be drawn because the defendant only mentioned the fact of the drug deal during cross-examination and did not volunteer it.
An adverse inference cannot be drawn because the defendant was not in fact silent during the police interview.

An adverse inference cannot be drawn because, although the defendant failed to mention a fact they now rely upon, at the police station they had not been given the opportunity to consult a solicitor before or during the police interview.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The defendant is charged with burglary. At the trial in the Crown Court, officers give evidence to the effect that, upon their arrival at the burgled house, they noticed that the kitchen glass window had been smashed and then saw the defendant hiding down a rear alleyway close to the burgled. The defendant was breathing heavily, sweating profusely and his trousers had a jagged tear. The evidence from the police officers at the scene is that they reasonably believed that the tear was a result of the defendant’s commission of the burglary. They also said that, in interview, after the standard caution about the right to silence, they had told the defendant of their belief that the defendant was down the alleyway because they had committed the offence and asked the defendant to account for his presence at the scene but the defendant refused to tell them. No other caution was administered. May the court draw such inferences as appear proper from the defendant’s refusal to account for the condition of their clothing?
options: No, because the defendant was not asked in interview to account for his presence.
No, because such inferences can only be drawn from failure or refusal to account for presence at the scene.
No, the court may not draw inferences from the refusal to account for the condition of their clothing.
Yes, because the court may draw inferences from their refusal to account for the condition of their clothing.
Yes, providing it is a fact the defendant could quite reasonably have been expected to mention which they now rely upon in their defence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.2: At the police station – interviews and advice: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crmp9.3.stem: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is under investigation for a number of frauds and has attended the police station voluntarily. The police have asked all the questions that they can for now, but they need to make some further investigations. The Custody Officer has concluded that the conditions for ongoing detention do not apply. There is a real concern, however, that the defendant may contact some of the victims and persuade them not to help the police. How should the decision whether or not to release the defendant on bail be made?
options: The police should grant bail without conditions.
The police should release without bail but with conditions.
The police should grant bail with a condition not to interfere with witnesses.
The police should release without bail.
The Custody Officer should remand in custody (subject to approval by an inspector) unless satisfied that conditions will be effective in preventing interference with witnesses.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been charged with the murder of their partner following a heated argument. Their solicitor has noted substantial evidence to suggest the defences of diminished responsibility or loss of control will apply. The police will have to make a remand decision about the defendant. What advice should the solicitor give to the defendant about the likelihood of bail being granted by the police?
options: The solicitor may be able to convince the police to grant bail without conditions by identifying the evidential issues, the defendant’s overall reliability given community ties and other matters.
Bail cannot be granted by the police because the defendant has been charged with murder.
Bail is unlikely because the defendant has been charged with murder.
The defendant will only be granted bail in return for their payment of a significant sum of money in the form of a surety.
The solicitor may be able to convince the police to grant bail with conditions by identifying the evidential issues, the defendant’s overall reliability given community ties and other matters.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for causing grievous bodily harm and burglary and is appearing before the magistrates’ court for the first time, having been bailed by the police previously. The court has just adjourned the matter to a later date. On which of these bases might the court legitimately refuse to grant the defendant bail?
options: There are substantial grounds for believing that the defendant might interfere with witnesses.
There are reasonable grounds for believing that the defendant might interfere with witnesses.
There are substantial grounds for believing that the defendant has on other occasions in the past breached bail conditions.
The offences are imprisonable.
Due to the nature and seriousness of the offence and the strength of the evidence against the defendant.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant was refused bail at the first appearance and has now attended a second hearing, at which the magistrates’ court has adjourned the case for trial and refused bail. Can the defendant apply for bail again?
options: Yes, but only if there is a change of circumstances and then only in the Crown Court.
Yes, but the magistrates do not need to hear arguments on facts and law in relation to bail unless there is a change in circumstances.
Yes, but the argument must now be made in the Crown Court.
No, the matter of bail is resolved and cannot now be reviewed.
Yes, and the defendant has one more opportunity to apply for bail in which the court must hear arguments on facts and law without any change in circumstances.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been refused bail on two occasions by the magistrates’ court but wishes to seek bail by appealing to the Crown Court. How will the Crown Court resolve their bail application?
options: The defendant can only raise matters not covered in their “certificate of full argument.”
The defendant’s application will involve hearing the matter afresh.
The defendant can only have the decision of the magistrates’ court set aside if it was not reasonable for the magistrates' court to make it (including legally wrong).
The defendant’s application will only involve consideration of points of legal error made by the magistrates.
The defendant can only argue new matters that were not argued in front of the magistrates' court.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant was arrested on a street late at night for with criminal damage and theft and has now been charged and remanded in custody. At the defendant’s first bail hearing, the prosecution expresses concerns that they are homeless and lack community ties, have no means of income and seem to suffer from alcohol dependency. They were represented by a solicitor at the bail hearing. What is the most realistic advice the solicitor can give the defendant about the prospects of being granted bail?
options: Bail is very unlikely in these circumstances as no conditions the defendant can realistically offer will overcome the substantial grounds for refusing bail in a case like this.
Although the court does not have to presume that bail is appropriate, any concerns the court might have in exercising its discretion can be addressed through appropriate conditions.
Bail is very unlikely in these circumstances as no conditions the defendant can realistically offer will overcome the presumption against bail in a case like this.
Although there is a presumption in favour of bail, there are likely to be substantial grounds for refusing it unless any concerns can be addressed through appropriate conditions.

Because there is a presumption in favour of bail, it is unlikely that there will be sufficiently substantial grounds for refusing bail once any concerns have been addressed through appropriate conditions.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been charged with common assault and criminal damage to the value of £2,500 (summary-only offences) following a dispute between neighbours. It is the first appearance and the defendant has been on bail so far. The magistrates are adjourning the case for trial and are considering bail. They decide there are substantial grounds for believing the defendant will continue to cause minor damage to neighbours’ properties. Are the magistrates entitled to refuse bail in this case?
options: Not unless the defendant was on bail when the previous offences took place or has failed to surrender to custody or breached bail conditions.
Yes, because there are substantial grounds for believing the defendant will commit offences on bail.
Not unless the defendant was on bail when the previous offences took place.
No because the defendant has not yet been convicted so bail must be granted.
Yes, unless suitable conditions are offered on the defendant’s behalf, because there are substantial grounds for believing the defendant will commit offences on bail.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been prosecuted for a non-imprisonable summary offence relating to food standards. The court has adjourned the matter for trial and is considering bail. The defendant has said certain things to the food standards officers during the inspection that cause the magistrates to think that the defendant might commit further offences before trial. In what circumstances can the court refuse bail in this situation?
options: Only if the defendant has previously failed to surrender.
Only if the defendant has previously breached bail conditions and the magistrates’ concerns about potential offences are substantial.
It cannot because the defendant has not been convicted.
Only if the magistrates’ grounds for their concerns about the potential offences are substantial.
It cannot because bail cannot be refused for non-imprisonable offences.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been granted bail pending trial for various indictable violence offences. The conditions of their bail include a curfew between 9pm and 9am and residence with their partner. The defendant is arrested drunk in a town 20 miles away at 10pm and brought before the court. They say that got into an argument with their partner and did not want to make the situation worse by “doing something stupid” so left the home. Which of the following best represents how the judge should deal with the situation?
options: The judge should not grant bail unless there are substantial grounds for believing that there will not be further breaches of bail.
The judge should remand the defendant in custody and will need to consider whether the defendant has committed the offence of absconding.
The judge must not grant bail because there is a risk of physical or mental harm to an “associated person”
The judge should exercise a discretion whether to renew or remove bail taking the defendant’s explanation into account.
The judge should grant bail unless there are substantial grounds for believing that there will be further breaches of bail.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant was bailed to attend court, which started sitting at 10.30am and has not arrived by 11.30am. The court has to move on to deal with other cases. Which of the following statements best explains the defendant’s situation and what the court might do about it?
options: The defendant has not committed an offence but has breached a condition of bail and so there will not be any presumption in favour of bail the next time bail is considered.

The defendant has committed the offence of failing to surrender if the prosecution prove there was no genuine reason for not arriving, faces an additional sentence in the case and has lost any presumption in favour of bail being granted in future.
The defendant may have committed the offence of failing to surrender without reasonable excuse and has lost any presumption in favour of bail being granted in future.
The defendant has not committed an offence until the court adjourns at the end of the day because it is still possible to surrender to custody on the day appointed.

The defendant has committed the offence of failing to surrender if the prosecution prove there was no reasonable excuse for not arriving, faces an additional sentence in the case and has lost any presumption in favour of bail being granted in future.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.3: First appearance and bail: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crmp9.4.stem: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant’s legal representative is seeking a representation order for their prosecution for criminal damage to the value of £120. The defendant has just started working as a solicitor. The defendant has no previous convictions and alleges that they have been wrongly identified as the offender. Assuming they pass the means test, which answer reflects the best appraisal of whether a representation order is likely in the defendant’s case?
options: The defendant does not require state-funded representation in the interests of justice because the offence will not attract a high sentence.
Because the defendant’s case may require expert cross-examination and because of a risk of potential loss of livelihood.
State funding is not required for a professional because the defendant should be able to represent themselves adequately.
While the defendant could probably represent themselves effectively, their case might lead to severe damage to reputation or loss of livelihood.
While the defendant’s case may require expert cross-examination, the offence is not likely to attract that high a sentence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted in the magistrates’ court for five counts of theft from the owners of a golf club where they had been allowed to do some casual gardening work by the owners. The defendant is homeless, otherwise unemployed, in receipt of benefits, has a significant number of previous theft convictions and is currently released on licence in relation to two other theft counts. Which statement reflects the likely outcome of an application for a representation order?
options: The defendant is likely to be eligible on the initial test but likely to fail on the merits test.
The defendant is likely to be eligible on the full means test but likely to fail on the merits test.
The defendant is likely to be eligible on the full means test and likely to succeed on the merits test.
The defendant may be automatically eligible on the means test and likely to succeed on the merits test.
The defendant may be automatically eligible on the means test but likely to fail on the merits test.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for multiple counts of fraud in their capacity as a chairperson of a charity. The defendant is employed once a week at a primary school in a self-employed capacity as a supply teacher. They jointly own a house with their partner, subject to a large mortgage and with very little equity. They also have a very small amount of savings, in the hundreds of pounds. The defendant strongly denies the allegations of fraud and there is likely to be the need for a forensic accountant to establish the defence they want to advance. The defendant is seeking a representation order for proceedings in the Crown Court. What is the most likely outcome of such an application?
options: The defendant is likely to pass the merits test and will have to pass the means test subject to the issues of contributions.
The defendant is likely to pass the merits test and will probably pass the means test subject to a contribution of income only.
The defendant will automatically pass the merits test and, because this is a Crown Court case, does not have to pass a means test.
The defendant may not pass the merits test but will probably pass the means test.
The defendant will automatically pass the merits and will have to pass the means test subject to the issues of contributions.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to a former partner and common assault on the partner’s new partner during the same incident. The defendant has appeared in the magistrates’ court for the first time. How will the court deal with each of these offences at this point?
options: It must send both offences to the Crown Court for trial on indictment.
It must commit the grievous bodily harm with intent to the Crown Court and stay the assault until the grievous bodily harm is resolved.
It must commit the grievous bodily harm with intent to the Crown Court and retain jurisdiction over the assault.
It must conduct an allocation hearing for the grievous bodily harm with intent and stay the assault until the grievous bodily harm is resolved.
It must conduct an allocation trial hearing for the grievous bodily harm and, if the grievous bodily harm with intent goes to the Crown Court, send the common assault with it.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Two defendants are jointly charged with a single count of burglary and theft and the magistrates’ court is determining which court to try them in. Both intend to plead not guilty and wish to be tried in the magistrates’ court but there are aggravating factors that indicate that defendant A will be sentenced to at least 18 months in prison. Defendant B looks likely to receive a sentence of about 9 months. How will it be determined where they will be tried?
options: The allocation decision will be made distinctly for each defendant.
The magistrates’ court cannot retain jurisdiction over the case because there are two offences to consider and, therefore, the sentencing maximum is 24 months.
Both will have to be tried in the magistrates’ court if the magistrates decide to keep defendant B there. Defendant A can still be committed for sentence.
Both will have to be tried in the magistrates’ court if the magistrates decide to keep B there. Defendant A can only be sentenced to a maximum of 12 months’ custody.
Both will have to be tried in the Crown Court if the magistrates’ court decides to send defendant A there.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is attending an allocation hearing to determine whether their prosecution for burglary of a commercial property should be tried in the Crown Court or the magistrates’ court. The likely sentence based on the facts currently available suggest sentence of about 9-15 months. The defendant would prefer the case to be kept in the magistrates’ court. What is the best advice that can be offered to the defendant at this point?
options: It is not going to be possible to persuade the magistrates to retain jurisdiction given the likely sentence.
It may be possible to persuade the magistrates to retain jurisdiction, in which case the defendant can only ever receive a maximum 12-month sentence.
The matter will be kept in the magistrates’ court if the defendant wishes it to be.
It may be possible to persuade the magistrates to retain jurisdiction but there is still a risk that the case will be committed to the Crown Court for sentence.
The matter must be sent to the Crown Court given that it is a burglary.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is attending a first appearance in relation to two counts of s 20 inflicting grievous bodily harm and has been asked to indicate what plea will be entered. The defendant’s legal representative asks whether they are facing a custodial sentence if a guilty plea is entered. How should the magistrates respond to this request?
options: They are not required to give an indication and cannot be restricted in imposing a sentence that is appropriate on the facts presented at the sentencing hearing.
They are not required to give an indication but if they indicate custody is not likely and the defendant pleads guilty at this point, they are bound by what they have indicated.
They are not required to give an indication but if they indicate custody is not likely, they are bound by what they have indicated.
They must not give an indication because they cannot restrict their decision before the actual sentencing hearing.
They should give an indication in order for matters to be dealt with diligently and expeditiously.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant has been excluded from the magistrates’ court after becoming abusive of court staff and shouting loudly at the start of proceedings. The court is scheduled to make a decision as to whether to send the case (two counts of grievous bodily harm) to the Crown Court.
