In what circumstances can the Magistrates’ Court proceed in the defendant’s absence at this point?
options: It can proceed to plea and allocation so long as the defendant is legally represented, it is not practicable to proceed with the defendant present, and if it is appropriate to go ahead without them.
Only in relation to allocation and only if the defendant is legally represented.
It cannot: it must adjourn until the defendant is able to participate in proceedings without disrupting them.

It can proceed to plea and allocation, even if the defendant is not legally represented, so long as it is not practicable to proceed with the defendant present and that it is appropriate to go ahead without them.
Only in relation to plea and only if the defendant is legally represented.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An adult defendant is due to stand trial at Cardiff Magistrates’ Court for assault occasioning actual bodily harm. Although the defendant can speak English, their preference is the Welsh language as the one with which the defendant feels most comfortable. The complainant is completely fluent in both languages and is happy to give evidence in either. What provisions are the court likely to make for the purposes of the trial?
options: There will be no provisions for language because all court proceedings are in English, and the court, because practicable, will be made up of English speakers only.
The defendant and complainant will have to give evidence in English, but the court will be constituted of all Welsh native speakers.
The defendant is the only witness who may give evidence in Welsh and the court, if practicable, will have at least one Welsh speaking member.
The defendant and complainant may give evidence in Welsh and the court, if practicable, will have at least one Welsh speaking member.
The complainant must give evidence in Welsh and the defendant give evidence in English and the court, if practicable, will have at least two Welsh speaking members.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An adult defendant takes a car without consent and drives it dangerously, before crashing it into a wall, causing damage estimated to cost £800 to repair. The defendant then ran away from the scene, before being arrested. The defendant is disqualified from driving and has no insurance. The Crown Prosecution Service decides to prosecute him for the either- way offence of dangerous driving and summary-only offences of criminal damage, driving without insurance, taking a vehicle without consent, failing to stop after an accident and driving whilst disqualified. At the allocation hearing, the defendant is sent to the Crown Court for trial. The other summary offences are sent to the Crown Court at the same time. Which, if any, of the summary only offences can be included on the indictment?
options: Taking a vehicle without consent and criminal damage but not the unrelated driving offences which should be remitted back to the magistrate’s court.
Driving whilst disqualified, driving without insurance and failing to stop after an accident are the only related driving offences charged that can be added to the indictment.
Taking a vehicle without consent, criminal damage and driving whilst disqualified are the only related and summary offences charged that can be added to the indictment.
None of them, because, although related, they are all summary -only offences which cannot be included on the indictment.
All of them because, although summary, they all are related offences and arise out of circumstances connected with the indictable offence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.4: Early trial procedures: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

crmp9.5.stem: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is accused of murder and it is alleged that they used a toffee hammer to kill the victim. The prosecution wishes to produce the hammer as evidence at the trial so that the jury can determine whether it was likely to have been used to kill. In what circumstances can the hammer be admitted at court?
options: It is admissible as real evidence but only if it is mentioned during the testimony of a witness.
It is admissible as evidence but only if proven as such by scientific evidence linking it to the defendant.
It is admissible as real evidence because of its relevance to the case.
It is admissible as real evidence but only if proven as such by other evidence.
It is inadmissible as evidence.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is being prosecuted for handling a stolen car. It is the prosecution’s case that the car was stolen and that the defendant was arrested driving it. The defendant’s solicitor does not want this to be a significant issue in the case because it might open up other issues that suggest the defendant’s guilt more compellingly (evidence relating to a wider conspiracy). The defendant does not deny that the car was stolen but claims at the time not to have been aware of that fact when arrested. How can the issue of the theft of the car be resolved in the defendant’s best interests?
options: The prosecution should be required to prove the fact as part of its evidence because the defendant’s solicitor should represent the defendant’s interests by not assisting the prosecution prove its case.
By the solicitor formally admitting the fact at court (whether the defendant consents or not).
By having the defendant admit the fact during examination-in-chief so that the issue is less damaging under cross-examination.
The prosecution should be allowed to prove the fact as part of their evidence because the solicitor should not be taking steps to mislead.
By the solicitor formally admitting the fact at court (with the defendant’s consent).
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant’s solicitor is appearing in the Crown Court and making a response to an argument made by the barrister appearing on the other side about the evidence given by a professor. Which of the following would be the proper way of addressing and referring to these people as part of an argument?
options: My friend has made a key point in relation to the professor’s evidence which Your Honour may think is ...
My learned friend has made a key point in relation to the professor’s evidence which Your Honour may think is ...
My learned friend has made a key point in relation to the person’s evidence which Your Lordship may think is ...
My learned friend has made a key point in relation to the professor’s evidence which you may think is ...
My friend has made a key point in relation to the professor’s evidence which you may think is ...
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is due to be tried at the Crown Court but has not appeared by the allotted time. What course of action can the judge take?
options: The judge should proceed in the defendant’s absence only if the defendant was too ill to attend.
The case must proceed in the defendant’s absence so long as the court is not aware of any reasonable excuse the defendant may have for being absent.
The judge may proceed in the defendant’s absence.
The judge may proceed in the defendant’s absence. The judge should proceed in the defendant’s absence but only if they have acted in a way that obstructs the course of proceedings.
The case cannot proceed and must be adjourned.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A solicitor is representing a defendant at the Crown Court on a charge of inflicting grievous bodily harm. As the jury is being selected, the solicitor points out to the defendant that the next juror in line is their neighbour, who the solicitor suspects of being hostile due to various neighbour disputes over the last few years. Can the solicitor do anything to prevent the neighbour from serving on the jury?
options: No, once a juror is part of the jury panel, this means that they have been properly filtered and selected and must be selected for the actual jury on a random basis.
They can only have the neighbour removed if the prosecution asks the neighbour to stand by.
Yes, but only if the prosecution agrees that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the neighbour will be biased against the defendant or that the neighbour is not eligible to serve on a jury.
Yes, but only if it can be established that there are reasonable grounds to believe that the neighbour may be biased against the defendant or that the neighbour is not eligible to serve on a jury.
Yes, but only if it can be established that the neighbour is not eligible to serve on a jury.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: The prosecution is making an opening speech in the prosecution of a defendant for robbery in a park late at night. Neither the victim nor another eyewitness have given particularly confident descriptions of the defendant, but their evidence is supported by fingerprint evidence and items found on the defendant when arrested soon after. How should the prosecution address the issue of identification during their opening speech?
options: They may outline the case but should not mention witnesses they intend to call.
They may outline the case but should not mention witnesses they intend to call and should remind the jury that they bear the burden of proof.
They may outline the case and the witnesses they will call, including the victim and other eyewitness but should remind the jury that they bear the burden of proof.
They may outline the case and the witnesses they will call, including the victim and other eyewitness. They do not have to mention the burden of proof.
They may outline the case and the witnesses they will call, including the victim but not the other eyewitness and should remind the jury that they bear the burden of proof.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A defendant is unrepresented in a summary trial, in which they rely on an alibi defence. The defendant gives evidence in their own defence and calls two alibi witnesses. The defendant does not know what the position is in relation to closing speeches and asks the court legal advisor for help. How should the court legal advisor respond?
options: The prosecution and the defence can make closing speeches.
The prosecution and the defence can make closing speeches. Only the prosecution has the right to make a closing speech.
The prosecution has no right to make a closing speech but the defendant does if not represented.
Neither the prosecution nor the defence have the right to make a closing speech because the trial is a summary trial.
The prosecution has no right to make a closing speech but the defendant does only if represented.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An adult defendant is on trial in the Crown Court for robbery. The allegation is that the defendant approached the complainant, pushed them and snatched the mobile phone from their fingers. The complainant has previously provided a statement to this effect and is the sole prosecution witness. During examination-in-chief, the complainant states that they are unsure about the push and, on reflection, think that this probably did not happen, but they cannot be sure. When cross-examined, the complainant accepts the defence suggestion that the phone was not in their hand at the time but rather on the wall where they were sitting. This is a case where the defence is entitled to make an opening speech if they choose to do so. What is the best course of action for the defence advocate to take at the close of the prosecution case?
options: Proceed with the defence case as planned.
Call no evidence so that you can proceed straight to your closing speech.
Begin the defence case using an opening speech to criticise the evidence of the complainant.
Make a submission of no case to answer.
Make a submission of no case to answer. Advise their client to plead guilty.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An adult defendant is tried in the magistrates’ court for a low-level shoplifting offence and is convicted by a majority of justices two to one. How much should the justices disclose when revealing their verdict?
options: They should explain why the verdict was a majority verdict.
The decision should be revealed by the justice’s legal advisor.
They should state their reasons in the form of a fully reasoned judgment.
They may give sufficient reasons to explain their decision, but they are not required to do so.
They should give sufficient reasons to explain their decision.
questions.subject: Criminal Law and Practice
questions.source: CRMP9.5_ Trials and trial procedure_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

disp8.1.stem: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An owner of a small business is in dispute with their business partner concerning the allocation of profits between them. They have stopped speaking to each other. However, the business relies on both of them working together going forward. They would not want their customers to discover that there is any conflict between them, as that would damage the business. Which of the following would be the most appropriate next step?
options: Direct negotiation between the partners
Arbitration
Mediation
Mediation Dissolve the partnership
Litigation
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An English company is entering into a commercial agreement with a counterparty based in a country that does not consistently enforce judgments of the English courts. The judicial system in that country is not considered to be independent and it scores poorly on international transparency and corruption indexes. The country is a party to the New York Convention. What jurisdiction clause would be most appropriate from the perspective of the English company?
options: An arbitration clause
An arbitration clause An exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of England and Wales
A non-exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the English court
An exclusive jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of the country of the counterparty
No jurisdiction clause
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A person is in a bitter dispute with their neighbour. The neighbour has started posting false and defamatory statements about them on a neighbourhood group chat. The statements have become increasingly serious. The neighbour has refused to stop and refuses to discuss the matter further. The person believes the neighbour intends to publish defamatory statements about them more widely. Which of the following dispute resolution options is most likely to be appropriate?
options: Without prejudice negotiations between the parties
Arbitration
Litigation
Litigation Early neutral evaluation
Mediation
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A company is in dispute with a supplier which they claim is in breach of contract. The company believes it is entitled to damages from the supplier. The contract, signed in 2018, is subject to the laws of England and Wales and contains a standard arbitration clause. Which of the following statements best describes the company’s options for dispute resolution?
options: The company is barred from taking any step unless it first attempts a mediation with the supplier.
The company can only commence an arbitration if the supplier consents.
The company can issue a court claim against the supplier in any circumstances.
The company can only issue a court claim against the supplier if the supplier is based in the jurisdiction.
The company must pursue its claim by arbitration and cannot issue a court claim.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A company claims it is owed £500,000 from a customer for the supply of goods. The parties have done business for years. The purchase agreement between the company and the customer has a standard arbitration clause. However, the company has issued a claim in the English court for payment of the debt. Which of the following statements best describes the legal position?
options: The court proceedings will continue because, as the claimant, the company can elect to issue a court claim or commence an arbitration.
The customer can challenge the court’s jurisdiction in the acknowledgment of service and then apply to stay the proceedings.
The court will automatically reject the claim.
The customer should file a defence and ask the court to transfer the claim to arbitration at the case management conference.
The court proceedings will continue because the court is the proper venue for a debt claim.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: Two business partners decided to have their dispute determined by arbitration. They agreed that there would be no option to challenge the award on any basis and the arbitrator should not provide reasons for the award. After the arbitration award is delivered, one of the business partners refuses to accept it. Which of the following statements best describes the status of the award?
options: The award is binding but it can be appealed to the court on a point of law.
As the award has not been agreed it is not binding.
The award is binding but it can be challenged by an application to the court if there was some serious irregularity in the arbitration.
The award is binding and cannot be challenged on any basis.
The award will not be binding until it has been reviewed and approved by the court.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: A firm has received a letter of claim alleging professional negligence. They privately admit that the prospective claimant received negligent advice. However, they believe the value of the claim has been inflated. No proceedings have yet been commenced. What advice should the firm receive regarding their options for dispute resolution?
options: A mediation should be proposed to try to reach a settlement or narrow the issues in dispute before a claim is issued.
Commence an arbitration before the prospective claimant issues court proceedings. That way, the dispute can be kept confidential.
Alternative dispute resolution would not be appropriate because the value of the claim has been inflated.
A mediation should be proposed to obtain a binding determination of the dispute on confidential terms and at lower cost than court proceedings.
Deny all liability, do not engage further, and see if the prospective claimant is willing to incur the cost of issuing a claim.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.1_ Options for dispute resolution_ Ghita Bennis (She_Her)

questions.question_text: An insurance company is in a dispute with a former franchisee financial adviser for breach of contract. The financial adviser has joined a competing franchise in breach of contract. The insurance company suspects that the financial adviser is one of a group of franchisees acting together but does not yet have evidence. They want to take robust action against any parties in breach of contract. In pre-action correspondence, the financial adviser has suggested that the parties agree to submit their dispute to arbitration. Should the insurance company agree to arbitration?
options: Yes, because the parties could select an arbitrator with experience in insurance matters.
No, because it is likely that the insurance company will want to join other parties into the proceedings.
No, because the insurance company will want to have the rights of appeal that are available in court proceedings.
Yes, because it will be significantly less expensive than litigation.
No, because an arbitration will not lead to a legally binding determination.

questions.question_text: A person has a claim for professional negligence and breach of contract in relation to negligent tax advice given by their accountant. The accountant is an employee of an accountancy business. The business is a limited liability partnership (LLP). The person engaged the accountant to provide the tax advice on the LLP’s standard terms. There are five partners/members of the LLP, none of whom were directly involved in giving the tax advice. Which of the following best describes the most appropriate defendant(s) for the claim?
options: All the partners
The employee
The LLP
The partner directly responsible for the employee
The insurer of the LLP
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A homeowner hired a structural engineer to advise on the building requirements for an extension. The structural engineer provided specifications for building works 7 years ago, which were relied on, and the building work was completed using the engineer’s specifications 3 months later. Two years ago, cracks started to form in the walls and a fundamental defect with the foundation was discovered. The problem has been traced back to incorrect calculations done by the structural engineer. The homeowner wants to bring a claim against the structural engineer in relation to the defective works. Which of the following statements best describes the status of the causes of action that might be available?
options: A claim for breach of contract became time-barred after 6 years but a claim for professional negligence still can be brought because the homeowner was unaware of any problem until less than 3 years ago.
No claims are available because it is more than 6 years since the structural engineer gave their advice and there is no evidence to suggest that they deliberately concealed their error.
Claims for breach of contract and professional negligence still can be brought because the homeowner was unaware of any problem until less than 3 years ago.

No claims are available because the homeowner discovered there was a problem within 6 years of the structural engineer giving their advice but failed to issue a claim before the end of the 6-year limitation period.
No claims are available because it is more than 6 years since the structural engineer gave their advice and breach of contract and negligence claims always expire after 6 years.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company had a dispute with a supplier. They agreed terms of settlement, which included an obligation on the supplier to make a payment of £10,000 to the company by 1 October 2016. The terms of settlement were set out in a deed of settlement executed by the parties on 1 September 2016. The supplier did not make payment as agreed. What is the last date on which the company can issue a claim for breach of contract?
options: 1 October 2028
1 October 2022
There is no time limit
1 September 2028
1 September 2022
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company is in dispute with a distributor that was appointed to sell their products. The company has terminated the distribution agreement. The terms of the distribution agreement provide that, upon termination, the distributor must hand back all marketing materials, may not market the company’s products any longer and must sell any remaining stock back to the company. The distributor refuses to hand back any marketing materials and the company is aware that they are still marketing and selling their products, in breach of contract. The company believes these activities are damaging to the company’s brand and will reduce their direct sales. Which of the following remedies might the company be able to claim?
options: Recission and damages
Damages, specific performance, and an injunction
An injunction only
Damages only
No remedies
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A restaurant owner has been dealing with a supplier of kitchen equipment for many years. The supplier has operated as a sole trader but transferred to a limited company 6 months ago and notified all their customers. The restaurant owner operates through a limited company. They are the sole shareholder and director. For cashflow reasons, they often pay business invoices personally and recoup the money from the company later. The only written terms with the supplier are from when they operated as a sole trader. The restaurant owner called the supplier and ordered a new oven one month ago. They personally paid an invoice issued by the supplier’s company. However, after taking delivery, an electronic defect is discovered making the oven unusable. The supplier refuses to take it back. Which of the following statements best describes the correct parties to a claim for breach of contract?
options: The only written terms are with the supplier as a sole trader. Therefore, any claim should be by the restaurant company against the supplier personally.
The restaurant owner paid for the oven personally, so they should be the claimant. The defendant should be the supplier company because it supplied the oven.

The order was placed by the restaurant owner on behalf of their company and accepted by the supplier on behalf of their company. The parties to the contract, and therefore the claim, are the restaurant company and supplier company, respectively.
The restaurant owner paid for the oven personally, so they should be the claimant. The defendant should be the supplier as an individual, because they confirmed the order on the telephone.
The contract was formed when the two individuals spoke on the telephone. The parties to the claim are therefore the individuals that agreed the contract on the call.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: Eleven years ago, a company director signed a contract with a supplier of computer equipment without reading it. The agreement charged ten times the market rate for the equipment to be supplied. The director deleted all copies of the contract from the company’s systems and made false accounting entries to conceal the sums paid for the equipment. The director retired from the board of directors 3 years ago. Last year, during an office renovation, a copy of the contract was discovered and brought to the attention of the board for the first time. Which of the following statements best describes the limitation period applicable to a claim by the company against the former director?
options: A claim can be brought against the former director but will become time-barred 12 years from the date of their error.
Any claims against the former director are time-barred because the error was made more than 6 years ago.
A claim can be brought against the former director because any limitation period did not start to run until their deliberate concealment was discovered.
Any claims against the former director are time-barred because they have since resigned from their position.
A claim cannot be brought unless the former director admits their error, which will reset the limitation period.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A local council wants to sue a road services company for damages for breach of contract. The company failed to complete a project almost 6 years ago and the council had to bring in another contractor and pay extra to have the work completed. The council’s solicitors wrote a letter of claim to the company 6 months ago and have just received a response from the company’s solicitors in which they suggest a mediation should take place before proceedings are issued. They have proposed dates for a mediation in 2 months’ time. Which of the following statements best describes when the council’s breach of contract claim should be issued?
options: The claim should be issued immediately after the parties attempt mediation (if they do not settle) – the company’s proposal of ADR pauses the limitation period.
The claim cannot be issued until the parties complete all the steps required by the Practice Direction on Pre-action Conduct and any applicable pre-action protocol.

The claim must be issued before 6 years from the date of the breach of contract, unless the council and the company agree terms of a standstill agreement that has the effect of extending the limitation deadline.
The claim can be issued any time – the limitation period no longer applies because the council has sent a letter of claim.
The claim must be issued before 6 years from the date of the breach of contract because issuing the claim any later will always be invalid.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company retained a firm of solicitors to provide legal advice on a contract being entered into by a subsidiary company. The parent company contracted with the firm and received and paid the invoices for the legal advice. The firm of solicitors gave incorrect legal advice, meaning that the subsidiary is unable to enforce the terms of its contract with a third party and has suffered loss. Which of the following statements best describes the causes of action that the parties may have?
options: Each of the parent company and the subsidiary company has claims for both breach of contract and professional negligence.
The only cause of action is a negligence claim by the subsidiary.
The only cause of action is a breach of contract claim by the parent company.
The parent company has a breach of contract claim and the subsidiary company has a negligence claim.
There is no cause of action.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person worked for a chemical company between 16 and 18 years ago. In the last 7 years, the person has experienced persistent headaches. They sought medical advice but no cause was found until 4 years ago, when further tests revealed a serious progressive nerve condition, of which the headaches are an early symptom. Medical advice received at that time indicated that exposure to certain chemicals the person worked with at the chemical company was the likely cause of the condition. The condition has become considerably worse over the last 4 years and the person wishes to sue their former employer. Which of the following statements best describes whether a personal injury claim can be brought?
options: Unless the court exercises its discretion to ext time-barred because the damage was suffered more than 3 years ago.
The claim can be brought because the person acquired the knowledge required to bring the claim less than 6 years ago.
Unless the court exercises its discretion to ext time-barred because the relevant events occurred more than 15 years ago.
Unless the court exercises its discretion to ext time-barred because the person had the knowledge required to bring a claim more than 3 years ago.
The claim can be brought because the person’s condition has worsened in the last 4 years.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: An ambulance driver, employed by the ambulance service, suffered serious injuries when they were involved in a collision when driving an ambulance. The collision was the fault of another driver driving dangerously. However, the driver’s injuries would not have been serious but for a defective seatbelt. The maintenance of the ambulance was outsourced to an independent company with a contract with the ambulance service. Is the ambulance driver likely to have a cause of action against the maintenance company?
options: Yes, because there is an implied contract between the ambulance driver and the maintenance company.
No, because the ambulance driver can bring a claim against the other driver or the ambulance service.
No, because all legal duties of the maintenance company are owed to their customer, the ambulance service.
Yes, because the maintenance company would have a duty of care to a driver of the ambulance they maintain.
No, because the ambulance driver does not have a contract with the maintenance company.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.2: Building a claim: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A wealthy businessperson retained a local small business specialising in interior decoration to design and manufacture furniture for their home. The relationship broke down when the contractor fell behind with the work. The businessperson decided to retain another company to finish the project at an additional cost of £15,000. It is clear that the original contractor provided a very poor service. The businessperson is aggrieved and wants to bring a claim. They say “money is no object” and they want to “make a point”, as the original contractor was inconsiderate and took on a job they did not have the resources to handle. After some heated correspondence between the parties, the businessperson wants their solicitor to issue and serve a claim, seek wide-ranging disclosure, and generally cause the contractor to incur as much legal costs as possible. Are these instructions likely to be consistent with the Overriding Objective of the Civil Procedure Rules?
options: Yes, because the parties have already engaged in pre-action correspondence. The instructions concern the conduct of the claim after it is issued, but the Overriding Objective only applies to pre- action conduct.
Yes, because the defendant has acted unreasonably by providing a poor service.
No, because parties are required to go through an alternative dispute resolution process before they are allowed to serve court proceedings.
No, because cases must be dealt with justly and at proportionate cost.
Yes, because the Overriding Objective is a directive for the court, not for parties.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A gardener has been sent a letter of claim alleging that they breached a contract to provide landscaping services at a country house. It is alleged that they supplied only half the plants that were promised. The gardener denies this. The gardener has spoken to their solicitor but says they want to ignore the letter and wait to see if the customer is willing to bring a court claim. Which of the following statements contains the most appropriate advice for the gardener?
options: No pre-action protocol applies to the claim, so the gardener is not expected to take any specific steps pre-action.
If the claimant is serious, they will have to write again before issuing a claim.
The court will expect the gardener to provide a response to the letter of claim setting out their position with their reasons for disputing any element of the claim.
It is up to the claimant to give the gardener an opportunity to settle but, if the gardener is not interested in settlement, the court does not expect them to sp decides to issue a claim.
The court will expect the gardener to make an offer of settlement in response to the letter of claim.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person intends to bring a claim against their former solicitor for negligence. Three years ago, the solicitor advised them on a claim against another party but failed to advise them to issue a claim form before the limitation deadline, meaning the claim became time-barred. The person has just instructed a new solicitor to advise on the matter. Which of the following statements best describes the next step that should be taken?
options: The claim should be issued and served.
A preliminary notice should be sent, briefly outlining the grievance, and asking that the former solicitors notify their insurers.
The letter of claim should be prepared and sent to the former solicitors.
The claim should be issued but not served until pre-action correspondence is complete.
A mediation should be requested.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A technology company is in dispute with a former employee. The employee was dismissed 2 days ago and, when leaving the office, they threatened to publish online a repository of confidential information of the company, including personal data of employees and customers. An urgent investigation has revealed that the employee downloaded a considerable portion of the company’s confidential information in the weeks leading up to their dismissal. The company wishes to pursue a claim against the former employee, including an interim injunction to restrain them from publishing the confidential material. The Pre-Action Protocol for Media and Communications Claims applies. It provides that the claimant should notify the defendant of their claim in writing, in a letter of claim, at the earliest reasonable opportunity, and that the defendant should provide a response before proceedings are commenced. Should the technology company follow the steps in the pre-action protocol before commencing proceedings?
options: No, because the former employee has made it clear there will be no settlement.
No, because the technology company needs to obtain an urgent interim injunction to prevent the release of the confidential information taken by the former employee.
Yes, because there is no impending limitation deadline, and the former employee is entitled to see the claim set out in writing before any proceedings are commenced.
Yes, because the parties need to attempt an alternative dispute resolution process before proceedings are commenced.
Yes, because the court will not hear any application for an interim injunction unless the pre-action protocol has been followed.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A person wishes to pursue a claim against their former financial adviser for negligence. Their solicitor has informed them that the limitation deadline is 1 week away. The matter has never been raised with the financial adviser. Which of the following statements best describes what the person should do next?
options: Issue the claim before the deadline, send a letter of claim as soon as possible and seek a stay of the proceedings pending completion of the steps in the Pre-Action Protocol for Professional Negligence.
Apply to the court to extend the limitation deadline.
Send a letter of claim as soon as possible and, if there is no letter of acknowledgment within the 21-day period set in the Pre-Action Protocol for Professional Negligence, issue the claim.
Send a letter of claim but state that a response is required within 7 days.
Issue the claim before the deadline and proceed with the claim in the usual way, because pre-action protocols only apply pre-action.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The owner of a party venue is the defendant to a claim for misrepresentation. The claimant alleged that they were shown photographs when making the booking that were not of the venue. When the claimant first wrote to the venue owner about their claim, the owner sent a one-line response: “We deny all allegations of wrongdoing”. They ignored further correspondence from the claimant. The owner has always been confident the claim is baseless, as it seems the claimant has mixed up photographs from different venues from which they must have sought quotes. The owner has the email where they sent the claimant accurate photographs of their venue. After the initial exchange of correspondence yielded nothing, the claimant issued a claim and it went to trial. The claimant has now lost the case. Is the owner of the party venue vulnerable to sanctions from the court for non-compliance with the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct?
options: No, because they responded to the letter of claim.
Yes, because they did not provide sufficient information to enable the objectives of the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct to be met.
Yes, because they should have proposed alternative dispute resolution.
No, because the claimant lost the case.
No, because the defendant has no obligation to prove their defence, the burden is on the claimant.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: The owner of a shopping centre wishes to bring a claim against a structural engineer for work in relation to an extension to the centre. The engineer’s drawings did not comply with building control standards. Therefore, when the extension was inspected, significant changes were required. This caused further work, building costs, delay in occupancy of several units and lost revenue. The owner followed the Pre-Action Protocol for Professional Negligence and is ready to issue a claim. However, they have discovered that the Pre-Action Protocol for Construction and Engineering Disputes should have been followed instead. Which of the following statements best describes what the owner of the shopping centre should do?
options: Make a settlement offer.
Issue and serve the claim form in the usual way.

Start the pre-action process again, by sending a new letter of claim referring to the correct pre-action protocol and follow the steps and timeframes per the Pre-Action Protocol for Construction and Engineering Disputes.
Apply to court for permission not to follow the Pre-Action Protocol for Construction and Engineering Disputes.
Review the Pre-Action Protocol for Construction and Engineering Disputes and try to follow any substantive steps not already followed, with reasonable adaptations and timeframes.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A large manufacturer of car components is in dispute with a car maker that has purchased their components for many years. A fault has been discovered with millions of the car maker’s vehicles, which they attribute to a component supplied by the manufacturer. If that is the case, the claim would be worth approximately £200 million. The component manufacturer claims the fault is due to an incorrect installation process for the relevant component, which is not their responsibility. In the course of pre-action correspondence, the car maker has proposed that the parties agree to a standstill agreement for one year, appoint experts to try to determine the precise nature of the fault and, if necessary, have a mediation thereafter. The potential cost to each party is estimated to be around £75,000. Is this proposal consistent with the Overriding Objective and the objectives of the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols?
options: No, because expert evidence should be sought only once court proceedings are underway.
Yes, because the proposal is reasonable and proportionate, in the context of a very valuable and costly claim, and may narrow or resolve important issues or the whole claim.
No, because the costs of pre-action conduct should be minimal.
Yes, because all evidence should be gathered and considered before proceedings commence.
No, because pre-action costs will not be recoverable by the winning party in the proceedings.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A company has sent a letter of claim to their former accountants, alleging negligence concerning the preparation of the company’s financial report 2 years ago. The solicitors acting for the accountants acknowledged the letter of claim within 21 days and sent a letter of response denying liability 4 months later. The letter of response was accompanied by a letter of settlement, written on a without prejudice basis. It includes a request for further information concerning the company’s alleged losses and a proposal of mediation following receipt of the further information. The company wants to press on with their claim without any further delay. Is the company’s intended next step consistent with the Pre-Action Protocol for Professional Negligence?
options: Yes, because the letter of settlement was written on a without prejudice basis and therefore the accountants cannot rely on it.
No, because there should be a negotiation period ending 6 months from the letter of acknowledgment, before proceedings are commenced.
No, because they must make an offer of settlement before commencing proceedings.
Yes, provided the company gives 14 days’ notice before commencing proceedings.
Yes, because the accountants did not respond within the required 3 months from the date of the letter of acknowledgment.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)

questions.question_text: A client has instructed their solicitor to write a letter of claim alleging breach of contract against a supplier of goods. They allege the goods did not conform to contractual specifications. The client has also instructed that a sum of £150,000 should be claimed as damages. This is not borne out by the available evidence, which indicates that damages are at most £50,000. The client insists that £150,000 should be claimed in the letter of claim, but agrees they would accept an offer of £40,000 or more and will limit the claim to £50,000 if it has to be issued with the court. Are the client’s instructions consistent with the Overriding Objective and the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct?
options: No, because the client should indicate in the letter of claim that they are willing to negotiate on the figure claimed.
Yes, because the client is willing to settle for an appropriate sum.
No, because a false statement in a pre-action letter can lead to proceedings for contempt of court.
No, because the claim form cannot deviate from the letter of claim.
Yes, because a letter of claim is not a statement to the court and the client proposes to give an accurate figure in any future proceedings.
questions.subject: Dispute Resolution
questions.source: DISP8.3: Pre-action conduct: Ghita Bennis (She:Her)
